utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Subotic, we are a little bit more distance compared to the day before yesterday. But I still can see you. Mr. Subotic I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the bundle be given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I'd like to take you to tab 4 of the binder. You see that document dated the 27th of April, 1992? For the parties, it's P1211. Shown to the accused on the 6th of June on transcript page 25258. Mr. Subotic n this letter you sent a request for reinforcements of the JNA 2nd Military District and I'll quote from this document. It reads, "In view of the essential need to bring the Territorial Defence in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to the basic level of manpower, in accordance with an agreement reached and a promise made in Belgrade, we request your urgent assistance in providing us with the following officers." Mr. Subotic, who has ordered or told you to issue such a request on the 27th of April?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prime Minister, since the existing units of the Territorial Defence had practically been deprived of the normal staff of other ethnicities that was there in peacetime. That is Croat and Muslim officers. So the staffs could not function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were referring in this request to an agreement reached and a promise made in Belgrade. Could you tell us what exactly you were referring to when you wrote these words?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That agreement was reached between the federal Secretariat for National Defence, to which a request was issued, since the previous TO units had been practically disbanded, to provide new staff so that we can avoid complete lawlessness. So we requested staff from them in order to fill our vacancies pending the establishment of the army and other structures in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And reference to a promise, is that that, when you discussed these matters, that they promised to send the reinforcement as you would request?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the negotiations that took place between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, or rather the federal Secretariat, it was agreed at the beginning that the JNA units, and this was also agreed with Alija Izetbegovic, that the JNA units would remain in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the next five years, and since no other army had been established, these units of Territorial Defence were some sort of formation that had to be harmonised. I personally did not take part in that agreement because it was reached before I took office. I took office on the 8th of April and that agreement had been reached earlier. I was not personally involved either in Belgrade or -- I was only informed and the whole government was informed that the agreement had been reached between the relevant agency in Yugoslavia, Alija Izetbegovic and the Assembly of Bosnian Serbs that was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would, then, the other party receive similar support or -- because you earlier were referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina; now you're referring to the Assembly of Bosnian Serbs in Sarajevo. Was this assembly a party to these negotiations or to such agreement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly who was there, who was involved, but I know that the Bosnian side also presented such requests, and I know from some later reports that President Izetbegovic demanded then that all Bosnian officers be sent from Serbia and other parts of Yugoslavia back to Bosnia. I know that but I have no written trace of that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did that result in all Bosnian officers sent back from Serbia and other parts of Yugoslavia to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, that was the outcome, with the proviso that a small number of officers refused. However, the majority of officers returned to Bosnia to their domicile, to their home places, from the Yugoslav People's Army, wherever they had been located before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything about the relationship between the Bosnian Serb government and the JNA prior to the formation of the VRS? You told us you took up office at the 8th of April. Until the 12th of May, how was the relationship between your government and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have good relations with the federal Secretariat for National Defence of Yugoslavia and I didn't have any personal contacts with them for almost three months, because I was not on good terms with them because I didn't agree with certain premises that had been proposed at the time. So I had no personal contacts. However, the government did contact with the federal Secretariat, mainly to request the JNA to protect the people, to calm the situation down in those first months, in that first month, because we had the bad experience of Slovenia and Croatia, where armed conflicts broke out spontaneously, and the government expected that the JNA would be able to defuse the situation and not allow internal conflicts. On a parallel track the assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina was trying to find a solution together with other parties in Bosnia. Discussions were going on, in which I was not involved but I was informed like everybody else, from the media, and I know that you know all about them because you have documents that cover all that. So the cooperation boiled down to the request of Bosnian Serbs made to the army of Yugoslavia to defuse the situation, not to allow interethnic conflict and to protect the people both on one side and the other side, and I must say that this was successful to a great extent. Let me just remind you of the incident when this part of the JNA was withdrawing from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You earlier said that you didn't agree with certain premises that had been proposed at the time and that caused your relationship with the JNA to be a bad one. Would you tell us what you did not agree with?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't agree with Blagoje Adzic, Minister of Defence. At that time his office was called federal secretary for National Defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you say that you did not agree that this man held this position or --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had nothing to do with him being in that position. It didn't concern me. It wasn't any of my business. I simply didn't agree with his attitude to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because we were persistently asking the JNA units that were already in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that had not pulled out yet. In fact, we thought that they failed to take the measures they could have taken to prevent conflict. That's what we disagreed on because I had expected much more, having been informed by the president of the republic, in other words the Supreme Commander, that there was an agreement between Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic and the authorities in Belgrade, that JNA units would stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a guarantor of peace, to prevent all conflict and war, and the time discussed was five years. That's the point on which I disagreed with the Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia because in practice they failed to secure that or they secured very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you ever receive any information that JNA units took part in combat activities at that time, where sometimes militarily, power was taken over in municipalities, sometimes not militarily but did you receive information as the involvement of JNA units or members of the JNA armed forces in such operations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any such report, not a single one, and I know that those units did not move at all until they received orders to withdraw to Yugoslavia. They sat in their barracks without responding to anything. I had no such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So according to your knowledge, they -- the JNA units stayed where they were, remained totally passive, until they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information, for example, of how -- no, I'm not going to further specify that. I'd like to take you to the next tab, tab 5. Would you please -- Madam Usher will bring tab 5 to you. That's P583, tab 23. And in the English, it's agenda item 10 on page 4, very top. And the B/C/S version, it's the page with the number 01245374. That's the semi-last page in the B/C/S version. You found it, Mr. Subotic? I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quote to you from this record of the government session. "The government has considered the proposed report. It has been concluded that the issue of prisoner exchange is extremely important, complex and delicate, and that if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. It has been agreed that a working group consisting of Professor Branko Djeric, Milan Trbojevic, Dr. Dragan Kalinic, Miso Stanisic, Bogdan Subotic and Momcilo Mandic, should consider all the aspects of the prisoner exchange problem and that they should propose systematic and other solutions, taking into account our international regulations. It is obvious that solving this problem is urgent and that the regulations and concrete measures for solving this issue should be proposed as soon as possible." Mr. Subotic, do you remember that this matter was discussed at the government meeting or at this government meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what prisoners were being referred to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was meant were prisoners that were taken on both sides in certain places, in municipalities, captured in the conflicts between those armed groups. As for me, by the 12th of May, let me just see this paper, I was working on the law on defence and the army, wherein I, as Minister of Defence, wrote in accordance with international law all regulations concerning the treatment of prisoners of war, and wherein I demanded, as Minister of Defence, because the law had just been finalised, and I provided a copy to the OTP, this law has -- includes special instructions on the treatment of detained persons, signed by me as the minister. It's on pages 189 to 191 of the law. That law came into force on the 13th of June. So, as you can see, this session was held just two days after the entry into force of that law. By that time, we already had some modest information, I would say, that prisoners were taken by both sides, and were being taken on both sides, in the territory of Republika Srpska. On a local scale, let me be clear; those were not major battles. They were other skirmishes, either planned or unplanned in my estimate, in which people were captured on both sides, and as soon as we received such reports, the Prime Minister proposed, since these regulations were already passed, to start enforcing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Subotic, you used the words, "Prisoners of war," you used the expression that people were captured. I think you said in skirmishes. You used the word "detained persons." You also told us that prisoners were taken on both sides on a local scale. A very direct question to you. Was this discussion exclusively about prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively those who were captured in skirmishes. At that time, we didn't call them prisoners of war at all, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has received quite some information that on both sides, that civilians, including sometimes women and children, were not free to move but were kept in conditions described sometimes in documents as a situation of detention or imprisonment. Did you ever see any such documents? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see documents about that, but I did hear that such things happened, and I absolutely condemned them as the minister, and I demanded from all governmental agencies and especially the army, once the army was established, to act strictly in accordance with the regulations passed into law. In addition to that, the president of the republic issued a special order for that purpose, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber is in possession of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you heard about that such things happened and you absolutely condemned them. Are you aware of any clear instruction that anyone, any civilian, should be immediately released rather than be kept somewhere for purposes of exchange?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not. I didn't give any such instruction, nor had I occasion to see one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it not have been appropriate, if a government or members of a government hear about these things to happen, to be entirely clear in their position, as you said, condemning it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. President, this working group that was established, at that time the communications were very bad. For the whole of May and June the communications, the communication lines with the local level were very bad and it was mainly messengers that brought us reports. It was really slow. However, this working group demanded that an order be issued and an order was issued to all municipalities, Crisis Staffs, et cetera, et cetera, that no prisoners should be taken, that the International Red Cross should be contacted immediately, and that both sides should immediately release those people who found themselves in so-called collection centres and whatever, because as far as I know, in Republika Srpska, there were no official prisons where civilians or any other people would be held. As for the local level and those temporary prisons they formed, I don't know what it looked like because I was not informed, but particularly with regard to civilians, the Ministry of the Interior received strict demands from this commission that these things be regulated and dealt with pursuant to the law, because these instructions pertained mainly to prisoners of war, men who would be taken prisoner in combat. It's the Geneva Convention that underlies this instruction. It didn't pertain to civilians, women and children, because it's not envisaged to capture women and children during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand from your answer that the working group was formed and did function. This -- you also said that they requested an order to be given that those held in collection centres, that both sides should immediately release those people who found themselves in so-called collection centres. Did you verify or did the committee verify or did you, as a -- in your position in the government, did you verify whether this actually took place, immediate release of those who found themselves in collection centres?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was not involved in dealing with this problem. I know that it was usually the Minister of the Interior who dealt with this, together with his organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you know, and whether you, or the committee, verified or let's put it broader, whether you in your position in the government, became aware of immediate release of all those who found themselves in collection centres.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally heard of the first case of this type when there was this collection centre in Prijedor. Up until that case, as a member of the cabinet and as a minister, I was not aware of any concrete cases. I was not aware of the existence of any such cases anywhere. Only when the collection centre was opened in Prijedor, that's when I heard about that collection centre. That was also made public, international organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina were made aware of that, and then action was taken with regard to that and you are familiar with the action that was taken in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're talking about the collection centre in Prijedor, are you referring to the -- we have several places in Prijedor where people were detained, at least that's what some of the evidence suggests, among them Omarska, Trnopolje, Keraterm? When you're saying -- when you refer to the collection centre you heard of in Prijedor, which one did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew of the collection centre in Trnopolje. I did not know about others. Well, later, I heard Keraterm being mentioned and Omarska, but I did not have occasion to obtain any direct information on this or to take any part in any of this. As a matter of fact, I happened to have followed the testimony of a Muslim here in this Court who was held in Trnopolje, Mevludin Sejmenovic was his name. It just so happened that I had the opportunity of seeing this on the internet, that he was released from that collection centre, that he went to Bihac, to try to find some opportunities for himself and he said then that there weren't any guards or barbed wires in the southern part of the camp. I mean, it was called a camp then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, testimonies of a witness will be evaluated by this Chamber, apart from -- if you would have followed these proceedings, I can inform you that some facts, some adjudicated facts, are before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, important is what this Chamber believes and it's not up for you as a witness to give your evaluation of evidence that was given before this Court. So would you please refrain from further doing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, it should be noted that Mr. Subotic is not reciting his recollection of that particular testimony off-handedly but has -- is reading from a document that he's brought with him apparently for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, did you bring a document? Because you -- I can't see it from here. Your desk is hidden by some monitors.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no. I haven't got a document. I just jotted down a sentence, the name of this person, who I saw on the internet. I don't have any documents, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if you write it yourself it still is a document. Could you perhaps just by showing it this way give us an impression of whether it's just one page or whether it's -- how many pages do you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have two pages but this is just one paragraph; the lady can have a look. The lady can have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it's in your language. Could we just have a look at the type of.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me I have the benefit of this particular angle and I was able to see that Mr. Subotic just removed that from another number of other pages he has. So if the question is how many pages he brought with him and how many are in front of him, it is more than two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, when I asked you how many documents, over how many pages you had, did you mover away some of those you had in front of you before?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just did it one more time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, how many pages did you -- Mr. Subotic, Mr. Subotic, how many pages did you have in front of you when you read a line --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a total of -- well, these are my own notes because I did not have enough time to prepare, three, four -- four pages. I can give the lady -- give it to the lady. She can have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is all you had in front of you --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I have, and also I have my own statements. I have my own statements and I have the law, the Law on Defence, and the army. I also had a video cassette which I brought, if some questions are put to me in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you should have asked permission to consult any paper work. Perhaps I have not been clear enough in instructing you to do so. But from now on, you're supposed to --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not know that I didn't have the right to take notes, bring notes, no one said that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, just for the record there were at least five pages that I saw there. I don't know if there are more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the number of pages that I just saw were five. So therefore that is then on the record as well. Could you tell us a bit more about what your role was in that working group, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role in this working group was the following. I was supposed to see whether the army, the army of Republika Srpska, took part in this, and since I prescribed instructions for camps, I was supposed to clarify what was required in accordance with the international law of war. That's my only role. I did not go into the field. I did not receive any reports. So that's it. That is only on the basis of what I heard from other people who worked together with me in the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were other detention situations discussed in this commission, in this working group, apart from strictly military? So what you said, "I heard about what happened on the local level, people being detained," was that ever discussed in this working group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this working group only worked in this particular case, only in this particular case. Later on, it did not have any permanent tasks in terms of controlling this. It was only supposed to investigate the situation that was present then, as far as the government was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "this particular case." What were you referring to? What particular case? Because it seems from the 15th of June government session, that it was not a case, but it was, rather, a problem of a more general nature, prisoner exchange problems. Now you say the working group discussed a case.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. President, here, in paragraph 10, the government looked at a particular piece of information to tell you the truth I do not recall what it looked like. Well, perhaps if I were to read it I could remember some of it. So there was this particular piece of information about this and we, as members of the government, were entrusted with the task of looking at this and proposing measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Subotic, you came spontaneously - I had not mentioned any specific case - and you said, Well, we only dealt with that specific case. And now I asked you what that specific case was and you said I don't know any more. So you had a whole working group dealing with one specific case, you remember that it was one specific case but ...

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot remember now whether it was the case in Prijedor or some other case. Believe me. I simply cannot remember it. It is not registered in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this order that immediate release from those in collection centres, who made that order and at what date?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the president of the republic issued that order. Well, now, I cannot, since -- well, I haven't got anything to see. As far as I can remember, on the basis of my statements from 1997, that these issues were examined. We certainly gave these orders to the Court. I know that orders were issued with regard to these so-called camps and other things, but I do not remember anything specific right now. To tell you the truth I didn't have it in my own hands, ever, so it's not really fresh in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would consult your notes, would that help you to find --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got that in my notes. In my notes I only have that case in Trnopolje. That's what I happened to see, this very brief thing. It was just a very brief report about the testimony of this man Mevludin and I jotted that down. I don't really have anything else. Because most of the polemics were focused on that, Prijedor, Trnopolje, Keraterm, was it a camp? Were pictures taken from here or from there? To tell you the truth I was not involved and I did not have any evidence about which I can speak in a relevant fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps during the next break the Chamber will have a look at what documents there are perhaps to be put to you in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Canivell has a question for you, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. We are not getting a translation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hear French now on the English channel. Could we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I try again? May I try again and I'll see if we now receive a translation? Yes. Paragraph 16 of your last statement, statement to this Chamber, you say that you heard that Mr. Izetbegovic had said he intended to create an Islamic state and that Bosnia-Herzegovina would become an Islamic state, and in order to do this, he made a statement in Tehran according to which he said that Allah had given the Muslims the right to use any possible means to fight against the infidels, those who were not of Islamic faith, and then you said that at that moment you understood that there was going to be a massacre of Serbs, a slaughter, and this would determine the conditions of a civil war. Could you explain to me what according to you would be the mechanisms according to which this war would break out? Would it be directly triggered by the attitude or was it the Serbs themselves who would start a war to prevent these intentions of Mr. Izetbegovic to become a reality?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really think about this, except that I read the Islamic Declaration at least ten times. Alija Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration. It had been published earlier on, a few years before this conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I consider there to be very dangerous, very extremist, both as a human being and as a professional soldier. It was clear to me that it was a type of threat. After all, Alija Izetbegovic, as far as I followed things at the time, at the joint assembly that existed, in the beginning, before the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina or somewhere around that time, when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as a state, he said roughly -- well, perhaps I cannot quote him verbatim but he said that he was prepared to sacrifice the peace for Bosnia. That is to say that on the basis of that, I made this proposal to the gentlemen who had talked to me that he should find the Islamic Declaration and read it for himself. It's not that I invented this. There are some other statements there too that were made public in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have a cassette here, a videocassette, an interview of a professor, Miroljub Jevtic from Belgrade, who studies the Islamic faith. If the Court wishes, I can hand over this cassette. Perhaps you can have it recorded too, because there are some other statements there as well that are perhaps not the subject of this hearing but they are the subject of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I brought this video cassette on purpose, because it is very specific, very argumented, well-founded, referring to periodicals and books that were approved by this government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I cannot remember all of that so I brought this cassette in so that I could proffer it to you if it meant anything to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, it would be highly appreciated if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. I want to ask you -- I would like to ask you what were your impressions at the time. The mechanism which would start such a civil war, would it have been either the Muslims who would have started this war or did you think that it would be the Serbs themselves who, anticipating an extermination which might be possible, would have triggered or started the war? What was your impression, the first possibility or the second?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood your question, Your Honour. As a professional soldier I was frightened by such statements such aspirations and I personally was absolutely convinced that there was a looming threat of a war that would be started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, later in the same statement, you say that, as from a given moment, it was obvious that Lord Owen was partial that he had sympathies on the side of the Muslims. All these things you mention before, these questions, the question of the targets, the objectives of the Muslims to convert Bosnia into an Islamic state, all these aspects such as partiality on Lord Owen's side, this question of a situation of confrontation between Muslims and Serbs, was this generally understood by a majority of Serbs, population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make any claims, but I know that in my own environment where I lived and worked, that is what people thought, practically without any exceptions. I can only assume that people in other areas also thought along those lines. After all, to this day, they've been asking for the abolition of Republika Srpska, this entity, and so on and so forth. They are not giving up on any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Eventually I would like you to refer to paragraph 35 of your latest statement, in which you say that even if General Mladic were possibly able to be in disagreement with Dr. Karadzic, nevertheless he had -- nevertheless, finally, he would submit to the direction of the leadership of Serbia -- of the Serbs of Bosnia, who would fix the objectives of the military operations. You reaffirm in this -- do you reaffirm this again?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that statement of mine pertains to the Igman operation. That is to say, there was a conflict between two sides, two armies. General Mladic with his units had an advantage. Lord Owen forced the leadership of Republika Srpska to stop that operation. That's when General Mladic quarrelled with the Supreme Commander. I'm saying this as a soldier. Every soldier in any army in the world has the task to disable the enemy and to reach the set objective. As a soldier, I believe -- and perhaps this is the only case, when I in my heart of hearts, supported General Mladic. Did I not make any public statements to that effect and I can could not have exercised any influence because I really did not hold any kind of office from which I could praise anyone or criticise anyone. But I'm saying what I felt in my heart of hearts and that is correct. I know that during the course of the war, many times the international community stopped actions of the Serb army, and I'm not aware of any particular case when the action of the Muslim army was stopped. I'm saying this as a human being and I have the right to say that because there are hundreds of pieces of evidence to attest to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But precisely what I'm interested in would be to know, when I asked my question was, not only to see if that had to connect with a particular fact of this operation of Mount Igman. What you say in this paragraph is couched in general terms. Do you still maintain this in these general terms, not only for the operation of Mount Igman but in general terms, do you maintain what you've written there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It did not pertain to everything else. I only had the Igman operation in mind specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another question I would like to ask. I'd like to know from you, as you say in paragraph 41 of the same statement, which you gave recently, well, what the military had investigated in all -- and pressed charges in all cases of violations of human rights, and that these courts had given about 300 judgements for crimes against Muslims or Croats. Do you know what are -- the trend was in these 300 judgements? Were those rulings which were sentencing or acquittals? Or what was the general direction of these 300 judgements?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had occasion to see those judgements. I mean, I had an overview of those judgements. They were issued by the military courts of the army of Republika Srpska. They issued at least 300 such judgements - maybe there were more of them later - pertaining to crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serb population, and if I remember well, I no longer have that paper, the military Prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska had contacts with the Tribunal and I believe he handed over those documents. Anyway, I know from those judgements that 90 [as interpreted] of them involved convictions, according to the laws that prevailed then. I cannot say that 100 per cent of them were convictions but I believe around 90 per cent were. I no longer have that file but I suppose you do because that was handed over to the Tribunal, and I know that the military prosecutor of Republika Srpska, later the military defender, had several contacts with the ICTY. I have no information, however, that there were similar judgements on the other side. So I cannot say one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have there been many cases in which the result was like Koricanske Stijene that is once charges had been pressed, finally the suspects were found or the accused were found and then after that, there were no -- were charges pressed or ...

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in detail what the outcome was, but I know from the public media that one of the protagonists of the crime at Koricanske Stijene was convicted here in The Hague. However, according to some unofficial information that I got through inquiries with the MUP in Banja Luka, I know that two of the participants -- there were three in all -- as I was told, got killed sometime during the war while serving in the units of Republika Srpska. As for these cases, those 300 judgements that I mentioned, they were not of that nature. They involved mainly one or two persons killed. I couldn't say exactly. There could have been some cases involving more than one or two but as far as I know, none of them involved mass murder. And I have no information as to whether those sentences were really served. I know sentences were meted out according to court regulations and laws. Whether the sentences were really served, I don't know, but there is no problem in checking that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seen the contents of these sentences? What were the penalties to which these persons who were sentenced -- what were the penalties? Do you remember? Were they long prison sentences or what were they?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, I remember -- I cannot tell you specifically but I remember nine, 8, seven, 13 years, something like that, but please do not -- I mean, I don't have that in my possession now. I just saw that overview. I had it in my hands. I'm sorry, if I had had time I would have looked for it in order to bring this paper, but I suppose that the Tribunal must have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your legal system or your criminal military system, there is a possibility of sentencing in absentia or if this person has disappeared, is it possible or not to give a judgement, sentencing that person?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I believe such a possibility exists, and that that was done, but I could not say for sure. I believe in principle it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you because you say, for instance, when you refer to the Koricanske Stijene case, that the people who were suspected and who were supposed to be three policemen, police officers, whose family members had been killed, that these three police officers, you say that they had escaped and they were charged but you knew that a bit later one of them had been found leading a normal life in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the centre of the Republika Srpska and was transferred later to this Tribunal. Do you have any news about the other two who were in the same situation or do you have -- do you know something about them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there may have been a translation problem in French but I just like to verify. In my English translation, I received as your testimony that the two others were killed in a combat situation elsewhere in Republika Srpska. These were the two you referred to, whereas the third, as you told us --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard unofficially, from unofficial sources. I did not have a document about it. But when this third one was tried, it was said that the other two had got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- perhaps there has been a translation problem. I'm usually listening to the English and -- so therefore you gave your testimony that the other two had died in combat. That's what you unofficially heard.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Judge Canivell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think there were other people? You say you don't know whether the penalties, sentences passed were applied or not. This is what you told us, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those military judgements? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. I have no other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know, sir, when you were in business, when you were in the government, did you hear about Milorad Davidovic? Ever heard about him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Davidovic? No. No. I can't recall that name. I know one Davidovic who used to be a minister but his name is not Milorad. I don't know any other Davidovics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you heard about an agreement concluded with the federal MUP, according to which the MUP would have sent Milorad Davidovic, with a group of police officers, to try and control and master the action of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You never heard about this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I'm taking you back for a moment to your statement about pictures taken and, as you say in your statement, that the people in Republika Srpska knew that it's been a setup, that the pictures were not taken in the camp but at another location. These pictures, did they cause any concern in government circles?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first -- you said they did not cause any concern. Now, you said that the people in Republika Srpska they knew that it's been a setup. Were people aware of these pictures -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most people believe that those photographs were a montage, and by the way the European press published such information, and that contributed a great deal to this public opinion prevailing in Republika Srpska, and in addition to that, the testimony of some witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm focusing at this moment on the moment when these pictures were published, not on later litigation on what was true or what was false in those photographs, but do I understand that when you say they did not cause any concern, that you are referring to that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, nobody believed that such a -- because this collection centre was not a torture camp so that it could turn a normal man into an emaciated one in just several days, because they had food, they were able to leave, and it was strange to people. They could not accept that it could be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you're talking about people, would that be the ordinary citizen of Republika Srpska as well? I'm talking about that time, not about now, but what they felt at that time. Did they not believe it at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that people who were around me did not believe it, and I personally did not believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you just said, could not be true because they had food, they could leave, et cetera. What was the source of your knowledge on -- that there was food, that they were free to leave, that they were --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the sources was that the people of Prijedor were saying so. Second, the collection centre was organised in the first place in order to shelter the population from the army or, rather, those fighters that turned up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The people from Prijedor, who is that? I mean --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizenry, the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that you were in direct contact with the citizens of Prijedor who told you what this was or how do I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, after the fact; that's what they said after. Not when this information appeared, but later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you before to focus exclusively on what you thought and what you felt at that time. So what was your source of knowledge when at that time you thought it could not be true because people would be free to go and people would receive food? What at that time made you believe that people got food, people were free to go in and out?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I don't have any arguments that I could substantiate my opinion with. All I can say is that all the information the government in Pale was getting, it was getting from the MUP and the municipality of Prijedor. I personally didn't see any reports, but that's what they thought after the information they got. I personally did not believe that somebody could be torturing those people in such stretches of time. I didn't believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were talking about a picture. Is it true that there were not only pictures but there was even video coverage of what happened, leave it apart at this moment whether that truly happened or whether it was a falsification?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was shown on television. Publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean also on Serbian television or Republika Srpska television? Could you tell us where it was shown?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And it was also in the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your local press, in your Republika Srpska press or --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely that man, the skeletal one behind the wire. He was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only the picture or also the video coverage of that moment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And video coverage, on tape, but you see, out of all those who were next to him, he was the only one who was thin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment about what was shown. I'm just asking when it was shown, where it was shown. Now, you tell us that you had reasons to believe that this was framed. Did in that respect -- was it -- were you aware that these pictures were perceived not in the same way in the foreign press, that they did not think that it was framed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know. I think his name is Mazovjtski, he was the one who was there. So, yes, I was aware. But it was odd that just that one man was on that photograph looking that way, whereas the others around him looked normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly the reason why I ask you whether you saw the video clip or whether you only saw one photograph. But now, this was -- this was --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I saw the whole footage that showed another dozen people, and that one is in the foreground. I don't remember his name. The thin one, naked from the waist up, whereas all the others around him were normal. They didn't look like him. They were not thin. That foot age was shown on TV, on Serbian TV, several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how did you appreciate that this was interpreted in the foreign media in a totally different way from how you interpreted those pictures? Did you have any specific reasons for not believing the interpretation that was given to these pictures in the foreign media?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have reason to doubt the veracity of that because Mr. Mazovjtski expressed himself in a very biased way in general and his cooperation in any matter with the Serb side was bad. That's why I have the impression I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mazowiecki, was he a reporter?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was some sort of international representative. I think he was a Pole. Maybe I did not properly name his position, but he had some kind of role there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like not to mix up official report and press reporting on certain events. I'm talking about a video clip or video coverage of something which you say was false, which is different from official reports to the United Nations. Did you -- did you consider any foreign publication, on whether it could be true or perhaps even if you came to the conclusion that it would not be true, did you consider on the basis of the content of that material, not just this video clip but perhaps also other information, further comments on what happened, whether it could be true or could not be true, what the foreign press was writing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not saying at all that it was false. Far be it from me to claim that. But that's what it looked like to me, and you asked me about my opinion and my feeling. I do not say that the collection centre did not exist. It existed and I condemned that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, that was not my question. My question was whether, when making up your mind whether it was true or not, and at this moment I'm not that much interested in the conclusions, but whether you considered what was published about or around this photo or video coverage, what was published about or around this in the foreign press.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know in detail what the international press and media published, but just that one thing looked suspicious to me, that that one man was so thin and the others were not. Otherwise, I am not saying that these things did not happen. I have no doubts about that, and I have no evidence to say that it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you able to follow a bit of what happened in the foreign press? You say, "I didn't see it in detail," but where did you get your general knowledge of what was published abroad?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when it was going on, I did not read about it. Later, when a debate started among the media, between our state and some other states, then I followed more of it. But at the time, I did not have occasion, and I did not have the opportunity to follow foreign sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "later," what -- when in time are you referring to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when the debate started and the trial and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean after the war? After the --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, one final question, as far as I'm concerned. You earlier told us about an order that everyone should be released from collection centres. In your statement you say, "I'd like to add," but that must have been at a later stage, "an additional order was issued by the president to check all these claims, to verify what was going on." And you think that this may have been in autumn 1992. That order sounds, in your statement, as an order to investigate rather than as an order to immediately release whoever is held in collection centres. Therefore, again, I'm trying to find out whether we have any specific order saying, "Immediately release whoever is detained in collection centres."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, just a few days after that publication was made, an order was issued to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then before we have a break, you offered a video. Mr. Subotic, we often take the approach that the parties can consider whether they think it of any use. I'm not yet convinced on the basis of your description, but I leave it to the parties to consider whether the video you have brought and which I invite you to give to the registrar so that a copy can be made, that the parties consider whether it would assist their case to present it to the Court. That's one. Second, and I'm now more directly addressing the parties. The parties are aware that this Chamber always has been very interested in finding records on serious Prosecutions and trials for crimes committed by Serbs against Muslims and Croats. Therefore, I take it if ever such a list of 300 judgements, which as far as I'm aware of I have not seen during this trial, I take it that if it exists, and if it's given to the OTP, that it would have been disclosed under Rule 68 to the Defence but I also did not -- I do not recall that we ever received such a list during the presentation of the Defence case. The witness says he doesn't have it any more. I'm in the hands of the parties as to whether such a list does exist, but not presented, or whether it is a phantom list. I've got no idea. But the Chamber is always, and I repeat that, very much interested to see whether serious attempts were made to investigate and to try Serbs who had committed crimes, serious crimes, against Muslims and Croats. If there is any information the Chamber would like and instructs the party to try to find it and to present it to the Chamber. Then we'll have a break, 25 minutes. We'll continue at quarter past 1.00, then have another three quarters of an hour until 2.00. We might discuss a few procedural matters to start with and then the Prosecution can examine Mr. Subotic. We resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to deal with some procedural matters first. And to that end, I'd like to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is still an issue of checking the -- of checking the translation of what Mr. Krajisnik said as a witness at page 26045. The Chamber is working on it, to have it resolved, the matter, so it's verified whether the words of Mr. Krajisnik were translated properly. That will be done on the basis of the audio and with the help of the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that, Your Honour. May I say on this particular point, Mr. Krajisnik himself has expressed special concern to me which I then pass on now to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but part of it was resolved about what he said about whether he knew whether it was Mr. X, yes or no, but this issue had not been resolved; I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then as far as scheduling is concerned, there was a request to have closing arguments to be heard starting on the 29th of August rather than on the 30th of August. The parties do agree on it. The Prosecution's request that the schedule be amended to start closing arguments on the 29th of August is granted. Then the parties are again urged to see whether they could provide the Kozarski Vjesnik article entitled, "Without censorship." The Chamber already asked the parties to see whether they could locate this interview. We have not heard since then. It might be of importance for the testimony to be heard next week to have that, at least, available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I clarify one thing in relation to what Your Honour said about starting on the 29th of August rather than on the 30th of August so that what the Defence has agreed is clear. We have agreed and there have been discussions, very friendly discussions between Mr. Harmon and me, as always. We have agreed that the Defence takes absolutely no objection to that one day adjustment from the 30th to the 29th of August but it is only that, Your Honour. The Defence should not, please, be understood as agreeing that either of those dates are in the overall context of the trial appropriate dates. It was that one day adjust document which we had no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say given the situation, the situation you -- is not in accordance with what you wished to be there, that the change of one day that you agree on that but you still think it proper to have it done in a totally different time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If it's going to be the 30th we have no problem with it being the 29th instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then these are the procedural matters I had on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I mention, I think it's D174 and 175. The Chamber has asked about the provenance of those documents. The answer is: The Mali Dom in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mali Dom in Pale, and that you said was the 174 and 175. Thank you, Mr. Josse for this information. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again although we have only 25 minutes, yes, because we'll sit until 2.00 and then resume at 3.00. So 25 minutes left until the next break. Perhaps I could ask the parties the following. A reference was made very often to a picture and a video which, as far as I remember, is not in evidence. I take it mainly because Trnopolje is very much about -- is very much covered by adjudicated facts. Nevertheless, it has been raised so many times and, of course, every one who is older than 30 will have seen it 50 years ago in newspapers anyhow so whether it would not be a good idea to -- but just to illustrate - not to establish anything additionally - perhaps to have that in evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I quite agree Your Honour and the Court is of course right that it had it not been for the adjudicated facts that information and much other information would have been available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Defence would take a different position, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like to know what is going to go into evidence. Perhaps I could discuss that with my learned friend, Mr. Tieger, and is see if we can come to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on my mind -- at least a picture which has been commented so many times and perhaps the video clip of which it's -- most likely is taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll direct ourselves during the course of our discussions specifically to that, and if there seems to be an additional material of the same sort of nature that would be of assistance, I'll of course bring it to Mr. Josse's attention and we will discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request at this moment is limited to this material but of course if you would like to discuss that, then there is nothing that prohibits you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I wasn't polite, paying attention to you when you entered the Court. You'll now be examined by Mr. Tieger who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to pursue in a moment at least one of the issues that the Judges were inquiring about earlier but one preliminary matter before I get to that. You testified at page 21 of Wednesday's transcript that you obtained "information related to the army and the leading of certain operations" and then mainly from reports received by the Supreme Commander which were forwarded to the ministry concerning certain issues. Now, you also noted in your interview of -- or your statement of December 1997, at paragraph 40, that you were aware that the Supreme Commander "always received daily reports from the field, MUP reports, police reports, army reports and reports of all the authorities and bodies. They had to report everything that people thought he should know about." Now, was your awareness that the Supreme Commander always received daily reports from the field, including MUP reports, police reports, army reports and reports of all the authorities and bodies derived from the reports that were -- that you received from the Supreme Commander that were forwarded to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any reports from anyone, but, for example, the Commander-in-Chief a few times or perhaps should I put it differently. Frequently, when things had to do with the Ministry of Defence, that is to say my own provenance of work, then they would call me in, in order to put some questions to me that only had to do with my own authority. As for other things, for instance, the Commander-in-Chief would forward them to the Prime Minister. These were things that were of a general nature and that had to be discussed in relation to the reports that he received. I did not receive any reports so I was not familiar with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, two questions and I'd like these initially answered yes or no if possible and then we can clarify if necessary. Number 1, you said in your statement of December 1997, at paragraph 40, that you knew that the Supreme Commander "always received daily reports from the field," and I listed those reports. Is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Number 2?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told the Court on Wednesday that your information concerning the army and the leading of certain operations was derived mainly from reports that the Supreme Commander had received and that had been forwarded on, that you had an opportunity to see. Is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm reciting your testimony verbatim. So from what sources then did you learn about information related to the army and the leading of certain operations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that reports were coming in because that was a procedural issue. However, I was not familiarised with all reports, but only that part of the reports, as I said a few moments ago, that had to do with my own provenance of work, or on the other hand, if part of a report would be interesting for the government, then as a member of the government I was in the same position, but by no means was I aware of all reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, speaking of reports received by the government, actually, it takes me to one of the issues that the Judges were talking to you about earlier. And that was the discussion that stemmed from the government session of June 15th at which the working commission was formed to address -- and I'll pull out that document, which is found at tab 5 -- to address all aspects of the prisoner exchange problem and propose systematic and other solutions. You said that the -- that your involvement in that concerned clarification of the laws of war. What were the other aspects of the prisoner exchange problem that were considered by Professor Djeric, Mr. Trbojevic, Dr. Kalinic, Mico Stanisic, and Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- well, the only reason was a mutual exchange of prisoners, quite simply. Well, first of all, let me tell you something. These people, especially in 1991, these people who were at local level, well, you know, it was imprisonment only conditionally speaking. In the simplest possible terms, they simply captured each other and set conditions for each other. They didn't really have any proper conditions or criteria. I mean this is what I think. This is my assessment. So quite simply, the reason guiding them was to have all of this resolved as soon as possible. That's just my opinion. I don't really have any information on the basis of which I could make any assertions to you because really --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suggest you do have information since you were on that working group. Wasn't the problem with the prisoner exchange the fact that the prisoners, the many, many prisoners, gathered in by Bosnian Serb forces were languishing in camps because the exchanges weren't going fast enough? Wasn't that at least one of the problems considered by the working group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, just the way you are asserting that, I am asserting to you that, as for that working group, I never went out into the field. I never had any assignments except to explain the provisions of international humanitarian law within that group that had to do with the treatment of prisoners. That's the only role that I had in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You spent quite a bit of time in the Krajina, didn't you, visiting the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, for the most part, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For example, you were present at the session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina of July the 17th, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me the venue where the session was held? Because I cannot recall the session now and perhaps I will if I hear what the venue was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll show you that in a moment but let me also ask you whether you were present in the ARK region on 4 August 1992, the day before international journalists entered Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Autonomous region of the Krajina, what was that? What assembly was this? Was it the people's assembly or -- I don't know what assembly you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then just take a look at this next document which is, I believe, P990. These are extracts from the minutes of the 18th session of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina held on July 17th, 1992, presided over by Vojo Kupresanin, attended by among others, General Talic, Goran Hadzic, Milan Martic, Velibor Ostojic, Dragan Kalinic and yourself, the Minister of Defence. And at that session there was a -- there were reports by Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Zupljanin concerning the current political and security situation in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You can see that under item 1. In addition, General Talic and Mr. Ninkovic and Milan Martic advised about the military operations of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zahar, during the course of your interview showed you a report prepared by Mr. Stanisic and submitted to the president of the Presidency and the president of the government on that very day, July 17th, 1992, in which he noted, among other things, as you heard during the course of your discussions with Mr. Zahar, that the army and the War Presidencies were gathering up as many Muslim civilians as possible and placing them into camps where, to say the least, substandard conditions prevailed. During the course of your discussions with any of the persons gathered at the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, including Mr. Zupljanin, what did you learn about the existence of facilities that held Muslim civilians in the region of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about any of that at that session. It wasn't at that session. Well, perhaps it was in the couloirs but not the session itself. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was not addressed on such issues by anyone. I remember that assembly. It was held in Banja Luka, at Banski Dvor. Now that you've reminded me I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You knew generally, at least, and we will talk about the specifics at the moment, what was happening in the region of the ARK. You knew about the military successes, you knew about the territories controlled by the Bosnian Serb forces, and you certainly knew something about what was happening to the Muslim population. Whether you learned it during the actual session itself or outside the session, tell the Court what you knew about that.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the session, I just heard what Talic said about the situation. I heard about the situation as he presented it but at that assembly session there was no reference to any taking of prisoners. No one talked about that. No one discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long afterwards was it before you learned that prisoners were being taken, that is Muslims were being gathered not in tens, not in hundreds, but in thousands by Bosnian Serb forces and held prisoner?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first case that I heard of -- well, I was in Pale at the time when I heard of that, and that was when some people were taken prisoner and taken to the camp of Manjaca. I think it was from that area -- well, the present-day territory of Croatia, I mean, up there in Kostajnica. I think it was from there. That was the first time that I heard of something like that. I was in Pale. I was not in Banja Luka, when I heard that existed. I put a question in this regard and I was told a that a camp had been established at Manjaca. I asked over there whether this was organised on the basis of instructions. Somebody made a comment saying, yes, it will be seen, some commission went out there. I was not involved in that. During the existence of that camp I was never in Manjaca. I know that there was this Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel who was appointed commander of the camp and so on and so forth and it was said that everything was done according to regulations. But I did not have any duties with regard to that. Another case that I learned of was this collection centre or camp, depending on who called it what, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you learn about the establishment of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that -- well, I don't remember the date, but perhaps a day or two after it had been established. I think it was pretty early on. I think that Kostajnica had fallen then, some fortification, I don't recall even the month, let alone the date, but after the fall of the fortification in Kostajnica, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many people were held at Manjaca during the course of its existence, at any given time and then throughout?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not recall. I do not recall any figure whatsoever. I did not have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You didn't make an effort to receive any information about how many prisoners were held at Manjaca? And no one made an effort to make you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I've already explained the day before yesterday that I was pretty much on the sidelines as far as the army was concerned, and the Main Staff and the corps. It was my understanding that that was not within my domain and I didn't delve into that. And that was on the territory of the 1st Krajina Corps; that is to say, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was in your domain, Mr. Subotic according to what you told us was logistics, including such things as food, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I think and I believe you made a point of telling the Court how it was your moral duty to tour around so that you could ensure that the soldiers had sufficient food and supplies. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to have an overview. In order to have an overview as to what the situation was. Not to supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But to direct your attention to the problem if in fact the soldiers were not receiving sufficient supplies, such as munitions, clothing, and food, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Whose responsibility was it to feed these prisoners in the Manjaca camp? It was not their own responsibility, was it? It was the army's responsibility, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the responsibility of whoever had set up the camp. But believe me, speaking quite frankly, from a legal point of view, I cannot tell you who it was that had set up the camp. Was it the military? Was it the police? I don't know. I think it was the army because the commander of the camp was a military officer. So my logical conclusion would be that General Talic had established the camp and therefore he was responsible for it. I did not have a single document about that camp in my own hands, not ever. Nor did I ever go up there. Everything I heard I heard either from the media or from some informal conversation, but nothing officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we break, let me show you at least one picture, and I'm going to show you some more of prisoners at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If this can be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You see that picture, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see this photograph and I saw it on television on TV Republika Srpska, precisely this one. The man in the middle, the one who is tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The two men on the side with those bony shoulder blades don't look too well-fed to me. Do they look pretty healthy to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. They don't look good to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Look at their condition carefully, Mr. Subotic. Wouldn't you say it is improper, indeed illegal, to hold people in detention and treat them in a fashion that results in a condition like that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were thousands of those people in Manjaca camp. It required -- the food to feed them, as you just noted, was at least General Talic's responsibility but ultimately it was the responsibility of those who were in charge and accountable for ensuring that the army received sufficient food to discharge its responsibilities, including taking care of prisoners, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that no one ever came to you and said, "We have thousands and thousands of prisoners in this condition and we need additional food to feed them"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that the state leadership had been informed about that, and then the president of the republic started a campaign to go there. He sent certain ministers there, of the Interior and I don't know exactly who all. And with the International Red Cross, and I don't know, some other international organisations, certain activities were launched but I was not aware of that. I was not involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have additional questions, of course, Your Honour, but I'm trying to be scrupulous about the time in accordance with the Court's instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider since the Court took more time this morning in putting additional questions to the witness, how to proceed. Mr. Subotic, your testimony was scheduled for two days. If we would not finish today, would you be available to stay over the weekend and be available on -- after the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can stay, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
