utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we have not yet decided on the matter and one of the additional problems would be that perhaps a videolink has to be used early next week. But we'll consider the matter. We'll now have a break until 3.00 and then we'll continue. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start, just for scheduling purposes, how much time would the parties need at a minimum? I add that. And whether that's your minimum or our minimum is still to be seen but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I of course begin with a customary caveat that it's always difficult to know. I will say that I attempted to craft the cross-examination along the lines suggested by the Court earlier, that is with the expectation of two hours. Of course, the hope that, if necessary, it would go longer but so that was what I was trying to do. I expected that I would have to truncate it, so I would estimate perhaps an additional two hours but maybe I'll be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I hope you will. Mr. Josse or Mr. Stewart? Mr. Josse, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to be cross-examining this witness. Your Honour, depending on how long the Chamber grants the Prosecution, I will do what I can to finish by 6.00 so long as the Chamber are not overgenerous to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. The Prosecution has taken until now approximately half an hour. You would like to have the same time as the Prosecution, is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ideally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, actually I said half an hour. That might be a bit too much. I could check it of course. We have a remainder of 2 hours and 50 minutes so including the time you took this morning, that would be a little bit more altogether for the parties, three hours; of course some time will be taken by a break. We'll try to keep that as limited as possible. Then let's try to -- let's see where each party would be able to finish in one hour and 20 minutes. And the Defence has used a little bit over ten minutes already. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sure the Court meant the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. It's Friday for me as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I'm going to try to move through this material as quickly as I can so I'll be returning to the issue that we were discussing before the break but let me address a few other issues first. During the course of your examination by the Chamber, you discussed some of the JNA activities that preceding May 12th. Now, this Chamber has heard considerable evidence, some of it from JNA documents, some of it from Bosnian Serb documents, some of it from other sources indicating that members of the JNA assisted in arming Bosnian Serbs before the war or otherwise assisting the Bosnian Serb military effort either before the war or prior to the establishment of the VRS. Did that happen or not, according to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, there were JNA officers -- let me take your example. You were a member of the JNA who, according to your statement, believed that Mr. Izetbegovic was a criminal, that he advocated that Muslims had the right to use any means possible against infidels, that he and other Muslims planned a massacre of Serbs, that it had been decided in Teheran to kill a million Serbs, and furthermore, that Muslims were essentially Turks. Now, what about those officers who fit roughly into that category? Did those people participate in assisting the Bosnian Serbs by providing weaponry, or participating in military efforts in any way before the establishment of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a republic in the former Yugoslavia, and most of the weapons of the JNA were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The reason for that are somethings in the pre-war years, the relationship with the Soviet Union, let me not go into any further detail. The Territorial Defence had its depot full of arms and ammunition and my conclusion is that when it comes to the first year of war, my conclusion can be applied to both sides, and it is my own conclusion which I cannot prove, I wish to say that both the Muslims and the Serbs used the depots in their respective territories and that they did not need any additional weaponry. I cannot prove that there were no private arrangements and so on and so forth; however, when it comes to the army itself, save for what the JNA had left when they were withdrawing, I am not aware of any organised arming in that first year of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, a lot of caveats there, it seems to me, organised and you may have said formal, I have to look for it. In any event let me be a little more direct. Didn't you personally engage in action before the VRS was formed to ensure that weaponry of the JNA was available to the Bosnian Serbs, and in particular, tanks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me personally. In Banja Luka, there were tanks that belonged to the school centre that I was the commander of, and some others belonged to the Banja Luka Corps, and the Banja Luka Corps did have some activities, for example, in Plitvice and some other activities during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to tab 15, please. If it hasn't been distributed, I would ask that it be distributed and other tabs be distributed. And tab 15, when it's received by the Court and the parties, is P64, P65, tab 128. Also P529, tab 49. And perhaps there is an additional page I think that can be distributed. I'm not sure we'll get there but it might be helpful. I'm directing the Court's attention to page 323 of the English. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking, page 176 of the B/C/S, Mr. Subotic. And this is Dr. Karadzic speaking at the 50th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. You'll see in tab 15 --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 176? I don't see that page. Ah, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And that's about ten lines down from the top, and in the English, Your Honours, it's the second paragraph beginning approximately ten lines down, where Dr. Karadzic says, "I want to say how it was at the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything," the Court is familiar with this passage, of referring to Variant A and B. You will remember the A and B variants, describing the B variant. And then, Mr. Subotic, we get down to the portion I wanted to bring to your attention: "The war began and the JNA helped as much as it could here and there. It had helped before. I hope this will not be going out on HTV. General Subotic helped just before the war began by sending tanks. He took the risk and signed for them to go for servicing while in fact he sent them to Banija. When Kostajnica fell we captured 300 to 400 Ustashas. It was done with the tanks of General Subotic who was a Colonel here." And then Dr. Karadzic goes on to speak more generally about the distribution of weapons and the organisation of the army by the SDS and that the armed forces, together with the police, were formed. Mr. Subotic, that's a reflection of your efforts prior to the war to assist the Bosnian Serb military effort in precisely the manner described by Dr. Karadzic, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. It is known and it has been recorded when the conflict -- that is not conflict but a crisis situation broke out in Kupres - this is a well known event - then the tanks from my centre went to Kupres, and their role was to separate the sides and no conflicts arose as a result of that and the situation lasted for some three or four months. However, those were the tanks from my centre, and what President Karadzic is saying about Banija, these were not the tanks from the centre but rather the tanks from the corps, and this is a fact, and this was registered, recorded, even filmed and it is no secret the JNA approved that from Belgrade, it was approved for the tanks to go to Kupres in order to prevent the -- a conflict. There was a colonel there; he was the commander. I can't remember his name, but this is the only thing that was ever done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic mistakenly thought that you were actually assisting the Bosnian Serb side when in fact you were just engaged in peacemaking efforts, is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also the JNA. I was a member of the JNA, and I was given the task from Belgrade to send that unit to Kupres. This was no secret. It was all legal and public knowledge. And there were no conflicts there. And as for Banija, those were the corps tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked a few questions about, I believe by His Honour Judge Hanoteau about your views concerning the imminent massacre of Serbs, the plan in Teheran to kill a million Serbs, the belief by Izetbegovic that Muslims had the right to use all means to deal with infidels. Was that your unique view among the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership? Were you, like, really the sole person who held that view or was that view shared by other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, all the people in the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs were aware of the Islam declaration and of the principles that are described both in the Koran and in the Islam declaration. I did not discuss those things with them but all of us listened to the speech of Alija Izetbegovic. Everybody listened. And Mr. Krajisnik listened. When Alija Izetbegovic spoke on the radio, when he addressed his fellow citizens, and when he said at the end, "Brethren you have to know that only the chosen ones can die for the Allah. Allahu Akbar." This was also recorded and I was clear when I heard that, and I believe that everybody else was clear as well as I was but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me -- okay. I appreciate you're trying to answer the question but let's be a little more specific. I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps before doing so, I would like to have a clarification of a previous answer about these tanks being sent to Banija. I understand your testimony to be the tanks of my school, they went to Kupres, that was -- these were different tanks. Which leaves that Mr. Karadzic says that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that was the JNA. That was the JNA, Mr. President. The corps was part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were sent to Banija, I do understand, and then Mr. Karadzic says that when Kostajnica fell, we captured three to 400 Ustashas, it was done with the tanks of General Subotic. Do I have to understand that he made a mistake there and this was done by the tanks of the 1st Corps because you said those tanks were sent to Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This it was a slip of the tongue. Both groups of tanks belonged to the JNA but I was not engaged on that side. I had my engagement on Kupres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand, but those tanks that were sent to Banija, were they involved in what happened in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kostajnica is in Banja. You go from Kostajnica to Dvor Na Uni and then you proceed towards Topusko and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Kostajnica came under the control of which party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in Croatia. This was the Croatian side. It was Croatia then and it is still Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When it was said when Kostajnica fell, it was done with the tanks of -- and now we have to say the tanks that were sent to Banija, under whose control was Kostajnica when it fell and who took at that moment with those tanks control of Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the control of the corps. As a matter of fact, it was under the control of Croatia because Kostajnica had a unit of Croatian forces, the ZNG forces. There was no major fighting there through [unintelligible]. There was just a -- the situation when the Croatian forces withdrew, some people were captured and from there they were taken to Manjaca, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question quite simply is what party took, with the help or with those tanks, control over Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not a matter of the Serbian side here and the others there because at that time the JNA still existed. It was not disbanded yet. This was the beginning and the composition of it was mixed but it was allied under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the parties could in any way enlighten me at a later stage on what actually now happened, it suggests - this language - that the tanks were used in support of the Bosnian Serb side to take control over Kostajnica. It's not entirely clear to me what it exactly is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war had not started by that time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know exactly what date it was that this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was during the months when there was all that situation in Plitvice. I can't remember exactly when. But the war in Bosnia had not started. The first conflicts were with the Croatian side. This thing in Kupres and the other thing in Banija, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, in your statement and during the course of your testimony, well certainly in your statement, you suggested that or indicated more explicitly that the TOs, that is the military forces before the formation of the VRS, were essentially self-organised and not directed or linked to any central body, referring here to paragraph 13 of your statement. This Court has received evidence, and I want to bring some of it to your attention and then ask you a quick question. P64, P65, tab 120, reflect the minutes of the national courts and government of the Serbian BiH from April 15th, 1992. I'm going to cite awe number of these. That one can be found at tab 4. That is a recommendation, it contains among other things a recommendation to declare an imminent threat of war and that you were temporarily appointed in charge of the TO. That same session reflects that in item 3, that the Minister of Defence shall order the use of the artillery and heavy weapons against the targets in the city of Sarajevo only when exceptional conditions justify such action. Tab 8 contains the minutes of the session of the NSC held on the 22nd of April 1992 and in the first item, strategic issues with regard to that item, it was agreed that the Serb Republic of BiH would maintain the positions that had been taken especially in Sarajevo and that Dr. Karadzic would coordinate commanding the TO. Tab 9 are the minutes of the session of the NSC from 24 April, in which a decision was passed on the formation of a Territorial Defence town staff from the former municipal TO commanders. Dr. Karadzic was put in charge of implementing the decision. Tab 11 is a session of the NSC on 28 April where the NSC adopted a decision to send a request for uniforms to the JNA. That is a decision was adopted on sending a request to the SSNO and the JNA General Staff to secure uniforms for the TO, and the ministry for National Defence is responsible for executing the decision. All of these decisions made during the course of sessions of the national Security Council and the government, Mr. Subotic, reflect the effort to direct those TO units that you claimed were self-organised and essentially independent, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 15th of April when this meeting took place and when the tasks were distributed. Before that, the units had already taken over their depots and whatever they had and this was no longer under any command and then this decision was issued to do something about that. A Colonel was appointed commander of the Territorial Defence because somebody had to organise things and to prevent anarchy from developing, and this was the situation until the 12th of May, until the army was created. This was just a temporary situation that we organised in order to prevent anarchy, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To prevent anarchy and direct the forces in the manner indicated in those minutes, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just to have somebody supervising them, to have somebody controlling them and establish a link. And that same thing was true of the Muslim side. Because the commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General -- whose name I can't remember at the moment, went to Belgrade. He just abandoned his post and left because there had been a commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we just filled the gaps in the organisation for the duration of a month, in order to prevent anarchy during that month. And this colonel coordinated the Territorial Defence Staffs in Sarajevo. He was in Sarajevo. He never went anywhere outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, there was considerable discussion during the course of your testimony on Wednesday about your -- what I understood to be, well, what you said was your personal, intimate opinion, having to do with General Mladic and what you "assumed without any" -- that's quote "assumed" without "any evidence" - that's at page 42 - about General Mladic. You also indicated at page 42 that you didn't know the extent to which Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic met, for example, because nobody invited you. But you did offer some opinions that prompted some questions about General Mladic -- the extent of General Mladic's autonomy or departure from Dr. Karadzic and the other members of the political leadership. Now, the best example you gave of any alleged conflict between the political leadership and the military, and you referred to it again today, if I recall correctly, was the operation on Mount Igman. Right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, the -- although you indicated to the Court that the operation on Mount Igman occurred in 1992, the fact is that that occurred in July and August of 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time there was a conflict between Mladic and Karadzic and I apologise if I was mistaken in the date, but there was a conflict regarding the end of those activities under the pressure of Lord Owen and so on and so forth. I may have been mistaken on the date because I'm not that clever to be able to retain for 12 years all those things that happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you don't -- I'll show you some documents, if I may, in a moment, but those events were in July of 1993. You don't dispute that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not contesting anything. If that is the case, that is the case, but that was the result of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the fact of the matter was, in that case, that the Bosnian Serb military forces launched an offensive which had the potential to take the high ground and control Sarajevo but air strikes were threatened by the international community and the Bosnian Serb offensive was also condemned by the Security Council; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's what prompted the decision by the political leadership to halt the offensive?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Pressure was put on Karadzic as a result of which Karadzic put a stop on the offensive and Mladic was against that, and Mladic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mladic didn't want to do it because it looked like the operation was succeeding but in the face of Dr. Karadzic's objection, General Mladic relented and stopped the operation, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that discussion, you were asked by I believe His Honour Judge Orie for any examples of operations in 1992 which were successful for the Bosnian Serbs, and which basically any operations in 1992 that were instituted against or over the objections of the political leadership, and you explained that at page 55, "you see, in 1992, there weren't any serious military operations except for the operation Igman." That's 55, 13 through 18. Now we know that now that the Igman operation was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court then that you, Mr. Subotic, the Minister of Defence, were not aware of any serious military operations in 1992 by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any of those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we take a look at tab 68, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this will need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise I'm at risk of going -- having to track back to get a number but I realise that the photograph did not receive a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes the photograph has not received a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, P1262 is a document dated 29 June 1992, to the 1st Krajina Corps command, sent by you, the Minister of Defence, Colonel Bogdan Subotic, extending "sincere brotherly regards to the brave soldiers and officers of the heroic 1st Krajina Corps from Banja Luka for the results achieved in the honourable combat to open the corridor. Hope and salvation for Krajina." You indicate your pride in the heroic deeds realised so far, and in the last paragraph indicate that you trust in God and the bravery of the 1st Krajina Corps for the victories to come. Does that document, Mr. Subotic, reflect or refresh your recollection about the existence of military operations by the Bosnian Serb forces during 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that the corridor towards Brcko and further on towards Bijeljina was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Subotic, I'm not look for an explanation of why Operation Corridor was instituted. I just want to know if you acknowledge now that there were military operations, serious military operations by the Bosnian Serb forces in 1992.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve babies died for the lack of oxygen in Banja Luka. This is a well known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, that is in already quite some evidence we heard before. Would you please concentrate on the question put to you and answer whether, where you said there were no major military operations, that being -- it's now been put to you the operation which created the corridor, whether this you consider this to be a major operation, military operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The road was made passable for the supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at tab 35, Mr. Subotic. That's P727, tab 18. This is operational directive number 4 of November 19th, 1992. And if you'll look through that quickly, you'll see directives to the various corps, many references to the liberation of territories or the protection of already-liberated territories, to the recovery of any lost territories, to the launching of offensive operations, and if you'll turn to page 5 of the English, referring to the Drina Corps, and in your version you'll see that under the directive to the Drina Corps, "From its present positions its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, Zvornik and the corridor while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population." You were aware of those offensive operations, weren't you, Mr. Subotic, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in Zepa, our soldiers died and I told you about that in -- but I have -- I have never seen any orders about any of the other operations but I was aware of the Zepa operation and I spoke about it in answer to Mr. President's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. You told the Court you weren't aware of any serious military operations, and yet serious military operations were occurring; serious offensive and liberating operations were instituted by the VRS throughout the second half of 1992 and you knew about that. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew then, but I could not remember. I only remembered the Zepa operation, no other. Of course, I was aware then of all these operations but I did not have any influence on any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Subotic, that any suggestion that might have been made by you during the course of your testimony on Wednesday or in your statement that General Mladic acted independently of the Bosnian Serb leadership is just -- in 1992, is just wrong, isn't it? The VRS and the political leadership pursued the same objectives and everyone was aware of the subordination of the VRS to the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. That's the truth, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suggest they are basically two questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start with the last one, Mr. Subotic. Whether everyone was aware of the subordination of the VRS to the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first one was whether the political leadership and the VRS pursued the same objectives. Is that true as well? Or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe in terms of plans, the answer would be yes, but in the implementation of these goals, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The specific question was about General Mladic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well then there are more than even two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I've now specified two questions. If would you like to get an answer on other questions that were all packed in one, you perhaps should --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It seems to me the same question, Your Honour, I don't know how General Mladic can be distinguished from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well weeks can ask Mr. Subotic. Mr. Subotic, whether we are talking about shared objectives and about whether the VRS was subordinated to the political leadership, would your answers include General Mladic as the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Yes. He was subordinated but the question was to what extent he observed these orders and to what extent he implemented them. That was within his own autonomous realm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand and were you asked earlier -- I asked you that question, whether you could give any example of 1992 where General Mladic -- so apart from Zepa and apart from Igman which was in 1993 most likely, whether you could give us any example on where General Mladic proceeded in a way which would be inconsistent with what he was expected to do by the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not say now. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of that subordination to the political leadership, the political leadership in Republika Srpska in 199 -- or the chain of command in 1992 had the VRS subordinate to the Presidency - correct? - which in 1992 was a collective Presidency, until December?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was subordinated to its Supreme Commander, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well the army according to the laws of Republika Srpska was subordinate to the president under the constitution, and under the laws on implementing the constitution, there was a Presidency until a president could be elected. You knew that, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was, yes. If those dates did not overlap with certain operations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And for the bulk of the second half of 1992, that Presidency was a War Presidency, and you knew that as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not called a War Presidency. It was called the Presidency. No official document said War Presidency. It said Presidency of Republika Srpska. At that time we had not had a declared state of war. We just had declared a state of imminent threat of war. That is official.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps we should not revisit the imminent threat of war and the state of war in full detail again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't intend to, Your Honour; I appreciates the guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you knew there was a War Presidency and you knew that for any number of reasons. You were present at the 22nd session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly when the existence of and continuation of that War Presidency was discussed at length. You were present at the session of the Bosnian Serb Presidency, one of three sessions of the Presidency, at which -- which you attended, when the retention of the War Presidency was discussed. And you yourself talked about the War Presidency at the 19th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't understand the question. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question is that in light of all those -- all that exposure to discussions about the War Presidency, you were very well aware of the fact that there was a War Presidency at that time, and that it consisted of the original three members of the collective Presidency, the president of the assembly, and the president of the government. That's the truth, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. But it wasn't called the War Presidency. It was the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, it was called the Presidency by most people but that's what it was. It was the War Presidency consisting of the people I mentioned, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say so, then you consider it to have been the War Presidency but it was the Presidency. That is official. In the constitution, in the assembly, in the documents that exist. So we cannot call it the War Presidency if it was not called the wards in the Official Gazette. I don't see why you insist on this word "war." We had not had a declared state of war. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, let's try to get to the basics. If you say someone couldn't call a body a War Presidency if it's not in the Official Gazette, then one thing may be clear, that I have seen human beings doing things which were not in the Official Gazette. So this kind of reasoning and drawing conclusions is perhaps not the best way to assist this Chamber. It was put to you that you even used those words, but let's try to get two matters clear and not confused. The first is how it was called, the president, War Presidency, or not, that's one issue. The second is how the Presidency or War Presidency, whatever name you give it, functioned in that year. Mr. Tieger has put to you that it was Mr. Karadzic, Madam Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, the president of the assembly, and the Prime Minister, Mr. Djeric, that those five people functioned as Presidency; whether you call them War Presidency or not is a second matter. Is that correctly stated by Mr. Tieger or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I know, it was only the three, Karadzic, Koljevic and Plavsic. They were the only members of the Presidency. The rest were there from time to time but I'm not aware of them being members of the Presidency and that is not mentioned anywhere in the Official Gazette. Djeric and Krajisnik. That's for sure. I know that they were not -- well, perhaps they were invited. I was invited sometimes to these sessions. But we were not members of the Presidency. The United Nations is aware of that too, and all of us who were in contact with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps next subject would be good idea. If you want to do that, to put to the witness directly words he used himself that might --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the 19th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And specifically to page 57 in the English, page 58 of the English and page 56 of the B/C/S. We found it, it's at tab 25. P583, tab 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You had an opportunity on Wednesday to see portions of this, Mr. Subotic. This is your lament about the fact that nobody informed you about anything, you don't take part in any decisions and little or no contact with the army Main Staff, on and on, and finally on page 56 of the B/C/S and page 58 of the English, the last sentence before the final paragraph at page 58, you say, "Anyway, I am probably the only Defence Minister in the world who is not a member of the War Presidency of the republic."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just a slip. Perhaps it was some kind of jargon and customary but I'm talking about official documents. Perhaps this was, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it doesn't really change matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you were asked earlier whether such a War Presidency existed and you were confronted with the use of the words and you said no one called it that. And then you refer to the Official Gazette. But now, it's now put to you that whether we found it in other documents, you said it never appears in documents, might not be the case, we have to consider that, but at least you yourself used at this occasion this terminology. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably so. This is a stenographic recording. I'm not denying it, but in principle it's a mistake because it wasn't the War Presidency; it was the Presidency. Now why did I utter this? Perhaps it was sort of customary jargon that we were not even aware of at that moment because in the Official Gazette and in the official documents of the Presidency of the republic, well, I don't know why you find that so meaningful. I really don't understand that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Don't try to pretend, Mr. Subotic, that that is a reference -- a slip of the tongue when you said "War Presidency" and simply meant the regular Presidency because, as you know yourself, it makes no sense whatsoever to suggest that you're the only Defence Minister in the world who is not simultaneously a member of the Presidency. It only makes sense in the context of a War Presidency, and you know it. That's right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let it be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, His Honour Judge Orie asked you about your testimony concerning the shelling of Sarajevo and how you could be so sure that Dr. Karadzic hadn't issued orders to shell Sarajevo and you assured him that you could be completely confident because you personally went through the Presidency archives in response to requests by this Tribunal and you didn't find any orders to shell Sarajevo. Right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I gave three books, three protocols, to Mr. O'Donnell and they selected the documents that they would take away. They themselves chose the documents. Among these documents there was not a single document that was like that. That is what I'm claiming. I'm not claiming anything else. If there was some secret order, well, but I don't think so. I don't think that there could have been a secret order that was not registered. I personally do not believe something like that, but I do not rule out the possibility that in some other way --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the logic of your suggestion to the Court is that if there had been shelling orders or other military orders of that nature, you would have found it in the archives, where you expected it to be stored?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also said at page 36 of your statement that Dr. Karadzic never issued any order to you said -- containing the words, "kill," "destroy," "burn," "slaughter," and I take it that two things, number 1, that referred to any orders, not merely containing those precise words but directed towards such activity, number 1, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And number 2, that was based at least in part on this search of the Presidency archives you talked about, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, because I worked on most of his orders, in pencil, the orders that he official -- that he did himself or, rather, that -- it was different when Mladic was preparing documents for him. That was not accessible to me. I am just confining myself to the decision that is the president reached himself and that he himself sent directly to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I am aware that you and your team didn't provide documents reflecting such orders to the Tribunal but I'm also aware that the Tribunal conducted a number of search and seizure operations to obtain documents that weren't otherwise provided. And let me show you one document that was located during the course of such an independent search and seizure operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could have that distributed and given a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, this is a document directive for further operations number 7, signed by the Supreme Commander, Dr. Karadzic, it's in March of 1995. And if I could direct your attention quickly to a couple of portions of that, first, to page 4 of the English at the top, and that would be in your version, the B/C/S, Mr. Subotic, page 6 or at the top of the page, you'll see the number 00823169, the tasks of the Republika Srpska army, and the last section of that first paragraph on page 8 of the English, "thus by force of arms impose the final outcome of the war on the enemy, forcing the world into recognising the actual situation on the ground and ending the war; 2, to improve the operational and strategic position of the RS; 3, to reduce the front line and create conditions for economic revival in the RS by sending a number of military conscripts home; 4, to create optimum conditions for the state and political leadership to negotiate a peace agreement and achieve the strategic objectives of the war." And then if we could turn quickly to page 10 of the English, and in the B/C/S, Mr. Subotic, that will be found on page 00823173, under the directives to the Drina Corps, last paragraph on page 10, beginning in the latter part of the -- just -- not the last sentence but the latter half of the sentence that precedes it, "While in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then quickly turning to page 14 of the English, and page 00823179 of the B/C/S. That will be at the top of the page for you, sort of the beginning of that, just before that second paragraph, Mr. Subotic, and, Your Honours, it will be the third paragraph from the bottom on page 14 of the English, "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits reduce and limit the logistic support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Now, this directive which refers to creating an unbearable situation, which orders, in fact the creation of an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa, Mr. Subotic, is a document that was not turned over to the OTP during the course of the search that you relied on to assure the Judges that Dr. Karadzic had never issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you nodding. Is that an affirmation of what Mr. Tieger just said, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say to the Prosecutor that this is a document of the Main Staff. It is not a document of the Main Staff. It is -- it was never in the archives of the president of the republic and I claim that with full responsibility, and also, your investigation team can confirm that. They had all the sealed protocols with all the marked pages. So it is a document of the Main Staff, and they prepared it and it was signed somewhere outside the Office of the President of the republic. There is the first time I see this. I know that there were some directives but this was never in the as of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were the Minister of Defence. You were special advise tore Dr. Karadzic. What's the point of assuring the Court that orders like this don't exist if they are not to be found in the Presidency archives?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that they are not there. I mean, I'm not denying or challenging this directive. I see that it is regular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I think the matter put to you is the following: In answering questions, you relied upon the absence of certain documents in archives you searched. Mr. Tieger now puts to you that the reliability of the absence -- that the absence of those documents as such, where important documents were found elsewhere - although you would expect them in such archives - limits the reliability of an answer that so heavily relies on what is found in archives. That's what Mr. Tieger puts to you. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just say that that document was never in the Presidency. It was never in the Office of the President of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think neither Mr. Tieger denies that, nor was that contested in the question I just put to you. Please move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before I move on from the Presidency archives, why don't you tell the Judges what happened with the Presidency archives when you were through with them? They disappeared, didn't they, and were not available to investigative bodies. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement in writing at the request of Mrs. Carla Del Ponte two years ago in relation to that and I will repeat to you what I said in that statement. That is correct. When the president, as requested, handed over this duty to Mrs. Plavsic he handed over the entire office, including all the binders with all the orders and documents that were in the Presidency. I was present there when this handover took place. I was present and the civilian chef de cabinet, Professor Micic, so the entire office remained under Mrs. Plavsic then. I stayed on, I continued to work in Mrs. Plavsic's office. Further on, in the month of March, the following year, we moved to Banja Luka, and Mrs. Plavsic was in charge. I don't know what she did with these presidential archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is, if they disappeared, it was -- it disappeared later, and not under our responsibility, because we transferred the archives once Mr. Karadzic has -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you give a long statement on that, these archives were transferred to the responsibility of Mrs. Plavsic, once Dr. Karadzic withdrew or at least resigned from that office. Okay. Did they finally -- do you know whether they disappeared after that? Whether they were not available any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They disappeared in Pale after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So they disappeared. And do you know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Disappeared. I gave a statement that the then newly appointed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you gave a statement. I want an answer to my question. Do you have any knowledge on how they disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. President. I do have knowledge. The newly appointed director of the police of Republika Srpska, in an action that was more of a political nature, and based on some discord among politicians, the following year, I think it was 1998, please don't take my word for the actual date again, he seized these archives. I absolutely do not know what happened to it. This gentleman later got killed. He was assassinated. So I really do not know about what happened to this and where this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Tieger, we have to finish approximately within the time limits set.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I had one more topic and I'll just indicate to the court I wanted to ask some questions about Koricanske Stijene. I'm at the court's disposal with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep it as brief as possible. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you indicated you reported to Dr. Karadzic about your meeting with Zupljanin and others concerning Koricanske Stijene. May I ask you to look quickly at tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 28, Your Honour, is P64, P65, tab 195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 27th Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1st of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Item 4, Mr. Subotic, as you'll see, it reflects that you briefed the members of the Presidency who are listed above about your visits to certain towns and military formations in the Bosnian Krajina and the wider area and informed the president of your military observations. Also indicates that the reports and conclusions were adopted in their entirety and you agreed with the order the president of the Presidency regarding the engagement of certain military formations in the forthcoming period. Is that the meeting at which you briefed -- you provided a briefing about your meeting with Zupljanin and others concerning the events at Koricanske Stijene which had occurred on August 21st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to look at two items quickly. Tab 56. P892, tab 84. This document is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps command intelligence and security division indicating that at about 1630 hours on 2192 and it is dated the 21st as well, that a convoy was stopped in the area of Koricanske Stijene, refugees were taken out, and genocide against the civilians was committed. In that connection, too, if I could ask you to look at the next document, I believe this is P892, tab 83. A report from the 1st Krajina Corps command to the Serbian Republic army Main Staff. On page 2 of the English, item number 3, indicating that a massacre against civilians, Muslim men, was committed on 21 August between 1830 and 1900 by a group of policemen escorting a convoy of refugees to Travnik. The massacre took place at Koricanske Stijene. Mr. Subotic, this event was clearly known to the intelligence and military forces of the Bosnian Serbs virtually immediately, as we saw from the August 21st document. Were you dispatched to, according to you, to Banja Luka to meet with Zupljanin immediately after the event happened and was made known?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As soon as the first signal reached Pale, on that very same afternoon, I left. I can't remember the exact date but that meeting in the Banja Luka MUP took place on the following day, but that was maybe two days after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that was a huge convoy, correct, many, many buses that travelled from Prijedor all the way through to Travnik, going through Banja Luka and other areas with the coordination of all the forces en route, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed of that. I didn't know how it was staged. I was only informed about the event that had taken place at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was not a secret convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many of those policemen who escorted or guarded the convoy were interviewed about what happened to what as it turned out were more than 200 Muslim civilians who were massacred?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was up to the judiciary and the civilian police, the MUP. The military did not take any part whatsoever in all that. I did not look at any of those reports. This was not my duty and they were not available to me, for that matter. I know that there was an order for investigation, for trial. This was all ordered to the judiciary and to the MUP. I don't know what transpired later on. I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think we nevertheless are at a point but I'll put one or two questions in this -- relation to this. When you were at this 27th session of the Presidency, when you briefed the members of the Presidency, did you tell them that over 100 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Presidency meeting, they had received an official report from the MUP. They had received a telegram and I did not have to mention any figures or what had been undertaken. There was a commission on the spot on behalf of the judiciary and the MUP. Measures were taken because the president insisted on those measures, on a trial. I did not mention any details. I just confirmed that it had been mentioned at the meeting in Banja Luka that the military units had not taken part in that, just the MUP and that the judiciary organs had taken the matter over into their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have any reason at that moment to believe that any of those present were not familiar with what -- with the event, with what was in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not have any reason, for that no fact or anything. Everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the conversation you understood that the seriousness of the matter was clear to all present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. And everybody was determined that this should be processed in a dignified way. Nobody was against it. I just conveyed the message from the president, who insisted on the strictest possible measures to be taken in keeping with the law and he insisted on a good team of people to deal with all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are about to close.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want -- one document, it's at tab 60, just have it marked, and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's have a look at that and then we'll finish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 60, Mr. Registrar, is a -- is a letter or a message sent by the chief of public security station, Simo Drljaca, dated 14th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's addressed to the security services centre, Banja Luka, to the chief. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Subotic, this is Mr. Drljaca indicating to the CSB that he was unable to investigate the alleged killing in Koricanske Stijene because the policemen were transferred to Han Pijesak and he's unable to provide a list of those persons who were travelling in the convoys. Are you aware of any investigative action undertaken after this point?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- no, I'm not aware of that in any concrete terms but the Court in Banja Luka should know about that because that case did come to court. I believe that the record still exists. However, I was not consulted in that matter after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about your awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break. We'll try to keep it as brief as possible. Mr. Registrar, minimum is, 18 minutes? We will resume at 10 minutes to 5.00, that's 15 minutes from now, sharp, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you'll now be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are not desperately pleased with the situation in terms of the time but we are determined to finish this witness today. Perhaps for future Chamber witnesses we can review the situation on Monday to make sure that this does not happen again. That's my first point. My second point is this: Mr. Krajisnik has literally just now indicated to me that he would like to ask one or two questions to this witness about one particular topic; in fact, it was the very last topic my learned friend cross-examined upon. We haven't had an opportunity he and I to discuss the matter properly, and in those circumstances, if the Chamber is, to have him ask questions on that particular matter and that particular matter alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a very sensitive issue. Therefore, let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you know that the Chamber would always prefer to have questions put by counsel. It will not disallow Mr. Krajisnik but first an attempt should be made by Mr. Krajisnik to see whether he can write down the two questions and if finally that would not result in you being in a position to put the questions to the witness, the Chamber will be very precise on the way questions are put. Of course we usually rely on your professionality as professional lawyers and counsel, and also in view of the sensitivity of the issue the Chamber will not be very flexible but will not disallow Mr. Krajisnik to put questions, if you see no other way to resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to start on another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exhibit P1263, Mr. Subotic, is the photograph -- you don't need to see it again. We are all sadly familiar with it. Can you recall when you first saw this image, either by way of this photograph, another photograph, or a video clip?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time on television but I really can't remember when. Because it was shown on TV many times. And it was also in some of the newspapers, but whatever I -- whatever time frame I could give you, I'm afraid I might be wrong. I don't know exactly how much later, after the fact, after it was taken, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm assuming from your answer that it was sometime in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really can't say. It's just that there is no wire fence on this photograph, whereas on the video clip that I saw, you could see the barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the video clip was shown and seen by people living within the Republika Srpska, was it a matter that was discussed, as far as you were aware, at a high level within the leadership of that entity or country?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was said about it at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, great doubts were expressed in the authenticity of that photograph, as I said in response to some of those previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just to go back to where I began, you are unable to say at what point in time that discussion, amongst leaders, took place? You can't remember now when the discussion first took place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked by the learned Judge, His Honour Judge Hanoteau, about someone called Milorad Davidovic and you said you did not know Milorad Davidovic, it was a name you hadn't heard of. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea who that person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think you were also asked about whether you had heard about agreement with the federal MUP that allowed Mr. Davidovic to control and master the action of paramilitary units and you said you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, if you would, please, at paragraph 37 of the statement that you prepared for the benefit of this Chamber. Do you have the bundle in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. You mean what I prepared just before arriving here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In paragraph 37, you talk about Vojin Vukovic, and approximately the middle of that paragraph, you say, "I later learned that the MUP arrested the yellow wasps because they were involved in some criminal activities. I know that Mico Stanisic did it. He's now in The Hague." Firstly, what did you mean when you said, "I know that Mico Stanisic did it"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it because this Vojin Vuckovic had committed a robbery. He had looted some valuable goods. I don't think it was weapons. I think it was money or jewellery, and he was generally speaking a problem. And President Karadzic tasked Stanisic to deal with it. So soon after that conversation that I had with him, where I lectured him that there could be no paramilitaries, he came to me to complain that he was being persecuted. I was however emphatic in my position and after that I learned that the Minister of the Interior organised his arrest and that he was arrested. I never heard of this Vuckovic man again. I don't know what happened to him or what became of him, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you have any idea how Mico Stanisic facilitated the arrest of Vuckovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at what juncture, if at all, did you become aware of the criminal activities that the yellow wasps were involved in?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had committed robbery of some gold jewellery or something, in the area around Pale. I heard something about it but no details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you have a look at this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't think this has previously been exhibited in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it needs a number. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm afraid, I don't think this has been distributed to the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But this is a report by a district public prosecutor, a Mr. Negovan [phoen] dated November 1993, requesting an investigation to be conducted against the Vuckovic brothers, and at the bottom of page 1 in the English, near the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S, we see a brief description of some of the appalling events that went on in the Celinac cultural centre on the 12th of June of 1992. When did you become aware of those specific events, if at all, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what is described in this document? You mean the event that the investigating judge dealt with here? I never learned about that, and I had no knowledge that he had anything to do with Serbia, with Sabac. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we are getting back to where I began with this line of questioning: You are unable to -- you have no knowledge of Milorad Davidovic's involvement in events involving the yellow wasps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the JNA and its involvement with the VRS. It's right, isn't it, that so far as remuneration of active-duty JNA officers serving in the VRS, you had some knowledge that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would remunerate them occasionally?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An agreement was reached between the Serbian leadership and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Serb leadership, in fact, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the effect that the federal Secretariat in Yugoslavia, since all the personnel files and documents of officers were in Belgrade, so it was agreed that they should pay the salaries of officers who had either stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina as natives of Bosnia and Herzegovina or who came back from Yugoslavia to Bosnia and Herzegovina because they were natives of BH. I can tell you that the number of officers paid by the army of Yugoslavia includes Atif Dudakovic and another officer, the federal Secretariat was then Blagoje Adzic. I don't know about the rest but I know about these two, Drekovic and Dudakovic because they were my officer I flew them and I knew them well and I know that they received salaries from Yugoslavia to 1993. Then Yugoslavia established the so-called 30th personnel centre so that all of us who come from Bosnia and Herzegovina were paid out by that personnel centre while being in Republika Srpska. But only active-duty officers were covered by this arrangement, not reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Both Mr. Dudakovic and Mr. Adzic were of --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were of Bosnian ethnicity both of them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I believe that some others received their salaries too. I have no specific information but I know about these two and also Mehmed Alagic, who was also one of my subordinates, a general, now of the Muslim army. He also received his salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the long answer that you just gave, did you mention that at time these officers were officers of the Muslim army, because it doesn't appear on the translation.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put it another way: Atif Dudakovic, which side did he fight on in the war?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Muslim side. And Ramiz Drekovic as well. They were corps commanders; in fact, commanders of the Bihac corps, both of them, and later they were promoted to even higher positions in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, briefly, I hope, to the issue of the so-called expanded Presidency. And I'd like to look at what you had to say about this in some of your earlier statements. In your 1997 statement, which I hope -- well, you may have it in front of you. It's only in English so you'll need my guidance. You say --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in English. So would you please read it? I have only the English copy. That's why I'm asking to you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I will do. At paragraph 49, in the middle of that paragraph, you say, in terms, there was no War Presidency at the republic level. And it's right, from what you said earlier, you obviously stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At paragraph 50, you say that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state of war was proclaimed a lot earlier than in the Republika Srpska. In fact the state of war was not proclaimed until the spring of 1995. And I don't think there is any dispute about that. You were then interviewed a couple of months later by John Ralston on the 4ing of February 1998 and at page 5 of that interview, you said, the middle of the page, "We had the Presidency of the republic. We had the Presidency that existed for about a year previously. I told you who made up the Presidency and they met every day." Now, it's not clear to me what you had previously said to Mr. Ralston as to who made up the Presidency but who did you have in mind when you gave that answer in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is written in the statement of 1997 but this was just a supplementary interview or questioning in 1998. Of course, when they typed out the transcript, they asked me to be interviewed again in 1998 and then they asked me these supplementary questions for the purpose of clarification of some answers given in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful but my question was: When you gave the answer, who did you have in mind as members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the members of the Presidency were the three, Karadzic, Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic, and it's written in the Official Gazette as well. There is no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally, we can see what you said at paragraph 21 of the statement that you prepared for this Chamber, so you do have that in your own language. You say, in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, "He was at meetings in his capacity as president of the assembly, so he was a very important figure. Also, there was the Prime Minister, there were members of the three-member Presidency so they had their own meeting. As for the expanded meeting when all of us were present, the Prime Minister and also the Minister of the Interior we discussed questions of everyday life, questions of survival, so on and so forth." Is there any question in your mind that what you were saying there was that there were only three members of the Presidency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's what I think. That's what I know. I don't know of anything different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, after a couple of questions were put on this matter but Mr. Tieger, I gave him the guidance that the Chamber would not be greatly assisted by further pursuing that matter. The same guidance is for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I ask one more question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- as I say, I'm not saying you can't put any more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, the Prime Minister of the government of which you were a member, did he ever say to you in 1992, Look, I'm not just a member of the government, the Prime Minister, but I'm also a member of the expanded Presidency? Did he ever say anything like that to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never said that and he never was that. All of us who were on the cabinet know that. He was invited to certain sessions but only to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I have made reference to the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997 and the supplementary interview in 1998. It is right, isn't it, and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, that Mr. Krajisnik is not mentioned in either of those documents by name?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is fair to say that in each, there is a reference to the president of the assembly. Obviously references to Mr. Krajisnik. Firstly in paragraph 30 of the witness statement and on page 4 of the interview. Mr. Krajisnik, we know, had not been arrested in 1997 or 1998. I dare say you know that, that he was only arrested in the year 2000. I see you nodding your head. The interviewers were clearly interested in what you could say about the chain of military command in the Republika Srpska. In your estimation, is the fact that Mr. Krajisnik is not mentioned by name in either the statement or the interview a reflection of how insignificant --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Asking this witness to gauge what the interviewers might have had in mind with --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The question is quite proper, Your Honour. I'm entitled to lead this witness as I please, as I want. I'm entitled to cross-examine him and he's entitled to comment on the answer -- beg your pardon, on the question I am just putting to him. There is nothing improper about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It calls for utter speculation about what may have been or may not have been in the minds of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's this gentleman's statement. He signed it. If my learned friend wants me to stick to the 1997 statement, I will do. He hasn't brought these interviewers here for us to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, on the transcript, the question is not yet finished. The Chamber is always a bit hesitant if estimates are asked from witnesses but would not preclude it. Could you try, Mr. Josse, to again and now in full put the question to the witness, also keeping in mind what Mr. Tieger said? I'm not saying that you're not allowed to put the question but I'll first listen to it in its entirety and then invite the witness to answer the question or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you only about the 1997 statement. You signed that as a witness statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you agree with my proposition that what the interviewers were interested in was the chain of command within the Republika Srpska? Did they ask you about that specifically?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Or were they interested in what the weather was in 1992? I'm sorry, excuse me for being facetious. You don't need to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They were not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your estimation, your opinion, is the fact that Mr. Krajisnik is not mentioned by name in that witness statement a reflection of how insignificant he was in the chain of military command in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I put my objection again and let the Court rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- you mean, Mr. Josse, both in questions and answers? No, the statement of course is just the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Only answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only answers. Yes, the witness may answer the question. Mr. Subotic, the question is whether the fact that the name of Mr. Krajisnik does not appear, whether this is in your view an expression of his unimportance, that he was not important in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely think that he was not important, because I know he was not important. It's not just that I think. I know. Nobody had to obey him and he had no right to order anyone anything. I know his job description according to the constitution of Republika Srpska, and as far as I know, speaking only in my own name, of course, but with full responsibility, he never addressed me any orders or any requests or demands that would have the nature of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The witness's answer can stand but in the future, I would appreciate it if counsel would not build false premises into the question. I see Mr. Krajisnik's name mentioned twice, at page 3. I haven't looked at any other page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I certainly accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because, as you said, you claimed that you could lead. You could not mislead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I most certainly accept that and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's look at these two passages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
