utterances.text: Also, of course, but that goes without saying that the answer will be interpreted by this Chamber on the basis and you might have made it a bit more difficult for yourself, Mr. Josse, by there because the witness answers on the assumption you gave to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me deal with it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik's name, I concede, is mentioned on at least two occasions in this witness statement. Does that change the answer that you have just given?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't change a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about matters which are alluded to on page 3 of that statement and also in other statements which perhaps I'll come to in a moment. You say at paragraph 9, where in fact Mr. Krajisnik's name is mentioned, "Between the 8th of April and 12th of May I participated in meetings with Dr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic and Professor Djeric, Professor Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik. We met quite often according to needs. There are some decisions from that time, mostly regarding organising living conditions in municipalities, supplies, breakdowns of communication, no telephones." My first question is: Where did these meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings took place at Pale, in the Presidency building. That's what we called that building. It was the so-called Kikinda building. It used to be a holiday place and that's why they referred to it as Kikinda.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And would you accept that the facilities that were available to you all were poor?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Very modest, very modest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that time, how did you assess the information that was coming from the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally received very little information from the ground. The Presidency did receive information of some sort, and when they invited us to their meetings, then they informed us about certain problems that existed on the ground. They asked for our opinion or proposals as to how to deal with such matters. Those of us who were not members of the Presidency did not receive information, because this was not provided for by any regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At paragraph 12 of the same statement, you say that Prime Minister Djeric chaired the meetings. There would be some meetings of only Dr. Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, and Krajisnik, and afterwards they would call Djeric and the Minister of Defence. We were in separate buildings. Where did these meetings, these joint meetings, take place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These joint meetings took place in that facility called Kikinda, in 1992 we even slept there, or at least a majority of us stayed there. As far as I can remember, Mr. Krajisnik also stayed there on the first floor of that building. There were some very small rooms there where we had short meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your witness statement to the Chamber, it is apparent in paragraphs 12 to 15, that you split your governmental experience into three distinct periods. The first we have just discussed, the 8th of April to the 12th of May of 1992. The second was the 12th of May of 1992 to the end of 1992. And the third was thereafter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. There are some very significant things, the situation changed significantly. First of all, we did not have all the bodies, then the army was set up. After that the Supreme Command was established. That is the reason why, as the laws were passed, as the solutions were found, the situation changed and moved forward in terms of organisation and in terms of laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about information from the ground, in the middle period, 12th of May 1992 to the end of 1992? It's right, isn't it, and, need be, I could show you a number of sessions, that the government was continually asking for more information from the army?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was a constant refrain of the government that they simply weren't being told sufficiently what was going on, on the ground, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They put those questions to me and I told them, "Gentlemen, I can't answer any of your questions. You have to put your questions to the army commander." And then the Prime Minister directly through Mr. Karadzic asked from Mladic - Mladic never attended any government sessions - and Djeric invited him. He wanted him to talk to the cabinet members. However, he did not hold any of us in very high regard, me included, and he never turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the Prime Minister ever say to you specifically, "Look, you're the Minister of Defence, you're going to have to do better. You need to try and rein in man in. You need to try and find out what he's up to." I'm talking about Mladic here. Did he ever say anything like that to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did tell me that and I answered him, and I state this for the record. I told him, the government and the assembly allowed Mladic to assume the role of commander and there cannot be two commanders. There is no army in the world with two commanders. The Supreme Commander and the commander of the Main Staff. And I told him, you are the ones who have allowed him to do that and I myself observe the law, the law on the army, and Mladic teamed up with the authors of the -- this law, the assembly, to pass such a law in which it is stipulated that I, as the Minister of Defence, did not have any rights or involvements with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the Prime Minister ever suggest to you that you should go and speak to Mr. Krajisnik, for him to intercede on your behalf with --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Never, never ever, absolutely nothing. Nobody ever suggested anything. Only when I resigned they all tried to convince me that I should continue performing the duty until a better solution was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't quite finish the question. What I was asking you is whether he should intercede on your behalf with General Mladic. You assumed I was going to ask about that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me to do that. Or at least as far as I know, I don't know whether anybody discussed this issue with the Prime Minister, without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where did your offer to resign fit in to the difficulty that you have just told the Chamber about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say how did that fit? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By that, I mean did your offer to resign have anything to do with what you had just been describing, your failure to have any control over General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Not only over Mladic but also the army. I said to the president when he commissioned me that I could not bear some of the things that he did and that had nothing whatsoever to do with the military rules nor with anything that we were taught at military academies and other high schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour we would next like to ask the witness a little bit about the Islamic declaration. Based on the questions both Your Honour and my learned friend Mr. Tieger asked the witness. There are one or two passages we would like to point to which indicate that the declaration states in terms what the witness said he feared was going to happen. I'm to some extent in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- I mean, is there any dispute as to what document is to be considered as the Islamic declaration? And is there any need, having heard the testimony of the witness, to ask the witness again? Or could the Court just read what it says and then establish by itself that this is what the witness said, or establish that that is not what the witness said? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can only presume that counsel is talking about the same document that all of us assumed to be the case. If there is any -- if there arises any dispute about that, we can deal with it. But I don't think there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if the only purpose of reading it to the witness would be to see whether what he said before we also find in that document, then the Chamber can read and the Chamber has heard the evidence and is, if you draw our attention to the fact that we should compare that and see whether it's reflected in that document; I think, as a matter of fact, that that would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would have the advantage of giving us the chance to send the relevant passages for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes that would be an advantage. And also I take it then that the document that will be sent, that the Prosecution will then also say that this is the document, always referred to as the Islamic Declaration. But I -- Mr. Tieger, yes. I take it that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour; that's a fine solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had one short question in relation to what you just asked. Mr. Subotic, you said that you resigned because Mr. Mladic did all kinds of things, not the things you learned at -- in the academy. Two questions. First of all, you also testified that the law was such that it was not within your responsibility, so what then made you resign? I mean, the law that was created was such that Mr. Mladic was not subordinate to you in any way. So therefore what he did was not your responsibility, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What you're saying is true. However, Mr. President, he simply eliminated me from his view. He acted as if I did not exist. I could not tolerate such humiliation. Not for myself. I did not desire power. I never wanted to be the commander in the army. And especially not in a religious or civil war, I would not have been a commander. However, he did not tolerate me for the mere fact that I did not lie to the state leadership, that -- for the fact that I pointed to some of his bad or wrong moves and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the bad and wrong moves you described earlier, what else would that be, what you would not learn at the academy and which was nevertheless, as I understand, within the behaviour of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way operations are conducted, the way the subordinated personnel is treated. My impression is that he treated his generals and those who are here in the detention unit as nobodies, that he never listened to any of them. That's my impression. I cannot prove any of that because I was not with him. I only know that a lot of them feared him and that they were his yes-men. They just said yes. Whatever he said they would just say yes, as if he -- if they had not had their own intelligence, their own brains, and I didn't like that. And that's why we parted ways, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you're referring to that when you said that he didn't act as you had learned at military academy; that is, the way he treated his subordinates. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is also true: That was just one of the elements and I could go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there anything else apart from personnel management and the way he treated people, the way he treated you, was there anything else in his behaviour that would not be in accordance with what you had learned at the military academy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he -- actually, I have the impression that he belittled the Supreme Commander, the Prime Minister, not to even mention other republican bodies. He simply ignored all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would not be the first thing I would think of, what you learn at military academy, but if you say that's it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, Mr. President, at the military academy, you are taught that the Supreme Commander is the Supreme Commander, and that all of his orders have to be carried out. There is just one exception to that rule. You cannot carry out an order of the Supreme Commander if that person is acting against his state. And that is the only exception to the rules whether it comes to orders and the execution of those orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're now talking about Supreme Commander are you talking now about Mr. Mladic or are you talking about Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'm talking about Mr. Karadzic, because he was officially the Supreme Commander. Although the other person was the real commander of the army; Mladic, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you were taught that the Supreme Commander is -- that all of his orders have to be carried out. And that is what you said in relation to the behaviour of Mr. Mladic, which suggests that Mr. Mladic did not follow the orders of Dr. Karadzic, and that's a question I've asked you before in different forms. To what extent, and where can we see that Mladic, General Mladic, did not follow the orders of Karadzic, therefore went beyond what he was expected to do? It's for -- it's not for the first time that I put this question but in your answers it is -- it comes back in some way, so again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, Mr. President, the best answer would -- to that would be provided by Mr. Karadzic, if he ever comes to trial. However, this is what I felt. This is what I saw. I have nothing to hide. That was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you have no examples of that. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to give any concrete examples?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what, for what? About the fact that Mladic acted independently, without consulting anybody? Is that what you're asking me? I can say -- I can share with you one of the most drastic examples, if you will. In 1995, on the 1st of May of that year, without consulting the Supreme Commander or any other state body, he called all of his generals and they signed the putsch against the state leadership. Every single general but for me signed that, and then they sent General Tolimir to put pressure on me to sign that and then I said, I am an honourable officer and since my Supreme Commander didn't do anything against humanity, I don't have the right to treat my Supreme Commander in such a way. This is just one example amongst many. And when this thing comes to trial, I offer my services as a witness. I will come, I will testify, I will prepare myself, I will find some papers and so on and so forth. I will not speak without documents off my head or just trying to remember things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, of course the beginning of the question was about what this witness did not like and what made him resign and what -- so therefore we are now in 1995 which of course is a totally different time issue -- time-frame, but Judge Hanoteau would have a question for Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, you have just told us that your impression of Mr. Mladic was that he treated his generals in a certain way. These generals, are those the ones who are here in prison? Are those the ones you refer to? You said that he never, never listened to anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This refers to those generals that are in prison as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have also said that you know that many of them feared him, that they were afraid of him. What did you mean by that? What did you mean when you said they were afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were not allowed to use their own heads to think. They were yes-men. They did what he told them to do. And that is something that was prevalent during the -- Tito's communist times. You did not have the right to think with your own head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm just asking what you did you mean when you said they were afraid of him, they feared him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were afraid of him. They did not dare make decisions without first consulting him. If -- and he never wanted to listen to anybody's opinion. He was arrogant. He had absolute power. He thought that he was the only one who had answers to all the questions, that he knew everything, and that nobody else knew anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You believe that the generals that were around him, or do you just mean the generals that were around him or the politicians as well? Who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the politicians as well. I believe that they also feared him to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that those generals who are in detention today, you say the generals -- you said exactly this: [In English] "My impression is that he treated his generals and those who are here in the detention unit as nobodies. That he never listened to any of them, that is my impression. I only know that a lot of them feared him and that they were his yes men." [Interpretation] Do you believe that those who feared him, at that time, were both his generals as well as the politicians who were in power at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite a number of the politicians also feared Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right that as far as you're concerned, the government in Pale did what it could to ensure the rule of law and respect international humanitarian law in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as communication is concerned, I want to go back to that for a moment, the situation presumably improved in the second period, from the 12th of May of 1992, when at least you had a number of telephone lines available to you in the Kikinda building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By the end of that year, how sophisticated was the operation of the Ministry of Defence in the Republika Srpska in terms of communication?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until 1993, it was rather poor. The situation improved only sometime in the first half of 1993. Until that time everything was on a very modest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that Mr. Krajisnik is content for me to ask a question or two about Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so and Koricanske Stijene is difficult to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very difficult. It's one of the reasons I was quite keen to have my client help me out, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your witness statement, the very last paragraph, paragraph 47, you talk about this unfortunate incident and you say, "I do not know about the Koricanske Stijene incident. President Karadzic received the report at Pale from the Banja Luka MUP about this event, so he convened a session of the Presidency. I think present were Presidency members, Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic and Mico Stanisic, MUP chief, and I don't remember if anyone else was there. It was really organised sort of on an ad hoc basis quickly." I want to suggest to you that you are correct when you do not include Mr. Krajisnik as among those people that were present at that meeting. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a real meeting of the Presidency any way. It was just a meeting, quite simply. On that occasion, messenger came to fetch me, said, you are wanted by the president of the republic, Mico Stanisic and I arrived together. The president shared with us the information he had received, and I could see that he was -- his greatest concern was whether the army had done it because he had no idea who had. So he told the minister, get ready, you go to Banja Luka now. He called up Mr. Zupljanin to tell him to organise both the police and the SUP and everybody to meet me. He told me that my mission was to establish whether the army had a role in it and to see what they had done about it by that time, and to convey to them that he was demanding the heaviest sentences, the heaviest possible sentences for the perpetrators of that crime. He was literally yelling because he had received calls from representatives various international organisations and he simply couldn't believe that something like that had indeed happened. There were no minutes taken and no records, it was not an official meeting according to procedure. It was an ad hoc meeting. I was supposed to leave that very night to be in Banja Luka the next day, to organise that meeting, because maybe a day and a half had elapsed since the incident. I don't know exactly, because I never made a time line. And the site of the incident was already cordoned off, taped off by the police and waiting for some state authorities to appear. And after that meeting, a team of judges from Banja Luka, including an investigating judge and I believe also the president of the district court, came and I don't know who else. In fact I remember there were three judges, there was Stojan Zupljanin, there were some other police officials, Simo Drljaca. They all went to the site of the incident. And later on, they reported to the president of the republic, to the head of state, along MUP channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have no reason to suppose, do you, that Mr. Krajisnik knew about this incident at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on that day, when I received my mission, he wasn't there. I don't know whether Mr. Krajisnik was there at all. I don't know whether he was at Pale at the time. I didn't ask about his whereabouts, and I don't even know when he found out, whether he found out in the days that followed after some reports were received, because some reports were sent to the Minister of Justice, and to other people. Some activity was taking place. So I don't know when he learned of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm out of time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would -- if you would have a few more questions, I know that it's 6.00 but I of course I would need -- it's not entirely in balance at this moment, unless you say, well, I've put the most important questions to the witness, of course, and you are aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I tried to tailor my cross-examination. I know there was another matter that Mr. Krajisnik wanted me to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if -- with the consent of the interpreters, and I usually -- when a party says time is over now, I usually do not encourage that party to continue, but given the circumstances and given also the fact that Mr. -- that we all tried to do our utmost best to finish with this witness today and also taking into account that the Prosecution -- whether there are good reasons for that is a different matter, had a bit more time than the Defence had, but if there is one issue you would like to complete, then with the assistance and with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How much more time do I have, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just look at the booth. Eight to ten minutes, would that be acceptable and then to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Eight to ten minutes would be okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a member of the government, I would like to ask you a little bit about the coordination between the government and the municipalities in the Republika Srpska in 1992. Firstly, to what extent were you involved in that sort of coordination?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved because I had some sections within the Ministry of Defence. In municipalities they were called sections of the Ministry of Defence. In Banja Luka in Bijeljina and in Sarajevo, I had districts of the Ministry of Defence. So those were my units of the Ministry of Defence. And I had coordination with them regarding mobilisation, personnel, record-keeping, purely personnel matters, because their job mainly had to do with staff issues. I have to say our communications were very poor, very poor indeed. They were on a very modest level, very slow, and that improved only in the first half of 1993. But we would write, for instance, to them that when MPs go to attend sessions of the assembly, they should take back post addressed to me, and that is the usual form of communication we had until mid-1993. And all the other ministers did the same. Maybe the Ministry of Police had the best communications because they had their police stations that were able to communicate amongst themselves, whereas all the other ministers were reduced to telephones or written communications sent by messengers or couriers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your 1998 interview, Mr. Ralston said at page 3, "Just one last question on that aspect. Was there any requirement that after operations, the military report back through the political side?" And you said, "Yes, of course, regular reports were sent, regular reports, practically daily reports, after the communication system was set up. I would say that that started in the beginning of 1993. Halfway through 1992, to the end of 1992 was based on what was possible but from 1993, we had communications between" -- "and then there was an unclear word -- we had daily reports." In that answer, you were clearly talking about military reports. To what extent did the same apply to reports to the government from civil authorities, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less it was the same thing. In other words, at the beginning of 1993, these reports of the civilian authorities were improved and before that time, it was through messengers who brought mail to certain departmental ministers, and I also believe that they were delivered to the assembly and so on and so forth, and that will be that. And the Supreme Commander received reports from the army, and to the extent necessary, he would inform the rest of us of some of the aspects and things that he believed that either the government or some other state bodies should be privy to. Those reports arrived at his desk and we could not obtain those reports unless he invited us to inform us about some developments that he deemed necessary to share with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The final topic I would like to ask you about is contained in paragraph 2 of your statement to the Chamber. And there, you talk about your contact with the Defence team of Mr. Krajisnik, and you talk about having a meeting with two Defence counsel in 2005, that you said I had nothing to add to what I've already said in the written statement. You then said they contacted me again this year and they insisted on me being a witness. Now, Mr. Subotic, this isn't in the least bit critical but it's a fact, is it not, that you were not very keen to come and give evidence on behalf of the Defence, for whatever reasons?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. First of all, I did not have contact with the two Defence counsel. There was somebody else and the interpreter. I may have been mistaken when I said two lawyers. I may have been wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to give evidence. It was me and an interpreter, wasn't it? And we met at the Hotel Bosna in Banja Luka. It was my sole --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. Yes. But I -- I forgot the way you look. Let me put it this way: On the order of Mrs. Carla Del Ponte and some other people in Republika Srpska, I was duty bound to provide the team of Mr. Krajisnik when they came to Bosnia or at least Mr. Niskovic was a member of the team at the time, with a written statements. We received a specific questions from the Defence and there was also Mrs. Del Ponte's order. Then Mr. Niskovic and the lady came to me I believe it was a laid abut that was not important. They brought those questions to me. They showed me this order by Mrs. Carla Del Ponte and I simply sat down and I answered those questions as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, if I may. I'm going to stop you because my question related to the last contact which was between you and an interpreter on our team, the earlier part of there year, where you, for whatever reason, and I emphasise I'm not being critical, you basically made it clear that you were not anxious to come and give evidence on behalf of the Defence. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall explain and I will be very honest. Your Honours, and all of you in the courtroom, in 2003 when the Milosevic trial was ongoing, Mr. Bernard O'Donnell called me. He was the head of the investigation team who interviewed me in 1997 and 1998. He called me personally, on the phone, and they asked me to come here because there were, as the interpreter put it to me, there were at least several hundred of questions that they wished to put to me. They asked me to come for an interview. That's what they told me. And then I said, at the office of The Hague Tribunal, I didn't want to do it on the phone. I'm a professional, I know what telephone communication means, and through the office of the ICTY in Banja Luka I established contact and I accepted to come here. Everything was arranged but I wanted my lawyer to be present, because I am here exposed and I knew that you would ask me all sorts of questions, and I'm not so powerful and so clever to be able to deal with the prosecutors, with the judges. "You can entrap me any way you want." That's what I said to Mr. O'Donnell. That's why I asked for my lawyer to be present to protect me. I had same request now, and since the ICTY did not want to cover the cost for my lawyer, who lives in the United States, and he has a Ph.D. in Anglo-Saxon law. Still I spoke to him and I accepted to come here and put an end to this never-ending story because I simply did not want somebody to think that I was afraid to come, that I did not respect this Tribunal, that I did not respect justice. And this is exactly what I told you on that occasion. And I told you -- I don't see after my statements given in 1997 and 1998 and you can obtain those statements because you're a lawyer, I assumed that that was the case and after the statement that I wrote down at the request of Mrs. Carla Del Ponte, I told you I don't see any purpose of me coming here to repeat all that in the courtroom. I apologise to the Presiding Judge, I didn't know that the living word is more powerful than a written word but I now understand that this is a fact. And if I had none that, maybe I would have behaved differently, if somebody had explained that to me. And then I told you in our second contact when you called me I told you, if I have to come, I still want my lawyer to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber is aware of communication between Mr. Subotic's lawyer and -- I think as a matter of fact that the Defence is aware of that as well. It has been always --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need more details on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't. Could I just ask -- this was leading somewhere, Your Honour, and it was leading to this question, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please lead Mr. Subotic. But eight to ten minutes are 12 by now so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You expressed a reluctance to come and give evidence on behalf of the Defence. Nonetheless, that doesn't diminish your respect for Mr. Krajisnik, does it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I respect Mr. Krajisnik. I never had any problems with him. I know him as a person. I know his behaviour. I know how he behaved during the war, after the war, I know how he behaved as a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I can say that I'm very sorry, very truly sorry that Mr. Krajisnik is in the situation to be charged with crimes. And this is my very honest opinion and I'm sharing this opinion with you with any -- without any doubt or fear whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Out of time for a second time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one final question for you, Mr. Subotic. You told us about meeting with those who were already informed about the Koricanske Stijene incident, where it was discussed and where it had to be, as you said, it had to be thoroughly investigated. In that period of time when this happened, did you have another meeting for example with Mr. Karadzic where you discussed this matter or is it once that you discussed the matter with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic, as you said, and I think Madam Plavsic that you mentioned. Was it once or was it several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only when I was tasked with that, and when I returned I just orally interpreted what I had done, what I -- what messages I had conveyed. I made a note of his order and I told him the Judges are on the ground, the police officers, the investigators are on the ground, nobody objected to that. I saw the atmosphere. I saw that everybody was of the opinion that this had been a terrible thing, that it was impossible for something like that to have happened. And so on and so forth. And later on, believe me, I did not follow any of that. I don't know how much was implemented. I only followed the media to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But when I'm talking about a meeting as you -- in your statement you say a meeting with Mr. Karadzic, Madam Plavsic, Koljevic, you said that the subject of that meeting was Koricanske Stijene, in a similar setting, did you discuss this once or did you discuss this more times? So not exclusively with Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Only once when I received my orders. And as for Mr. Karadzic, I just submitted my report to him on my return. However, he had already had written reports from the MUP and from other sources, for example, the Court, I suppose. So the report that I submitted to him was no longer very important. I just told him what I had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm a little confused, Your Honour. The Court referred to the tasking that this witness referred to. I had specifically asked him about the reporting back that he referred to in his statement and I directed him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was mainly concerned -- well, let's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber feels no need to further expand on this matter at this moment, Mr. -- this then concludes your testimony, Mr. Subotic. First of all, we would like to return to you the video you were so kind to give to this Tribunal, which has been copied and which has been or will be made available to the parties. I'd like to thank you very much for coming your long way to The Hague and to answer the questions of this Bench, of both parties, and I wish you a safe trip home again. We adjourn until next Monday, 9.00, Courtroom II, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Courtroom I, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Courtroom I, next Monday. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24
